Phil Hagelberg <phil@hagelb.org> writes:

> This phenomenon is known as the "vibe bobsled", and it's been well
> documented; even people who are enthusiastic LLM users admit it happens:
>
> https://dustycloud.org/blog/faulty-towers-vibe-sickness-and-the-vibe-bobsled/

> [...]

> I know this looks at first glance like a slippery slope fallacy, but I'm
> just describing what happened from painful firsthand personal experience.

(I'm the author of the quoted blogpost)

On that note, the observation discussed in the blogpost of a growing
amount of code that nobody understands leading to eventually
surrendering to the LLM to explain things came from an LLM *proponent*,
which I used as the frame. Whereas I described a bobsled, the original
proponent described a growing tower... Armin Ronacher, one of the
biggest generative AI via LLM in coding proponents currently around
wrote a blogpost called "The Tower Keeps Rising":

  https://lucumr.pocoo.org/2026/7/13/the-tower-keeps-rising/

In it, Armin describes that AI-assisted codebases eventually become
incomprehensible to human participants, and that they keep growing,
and this is not unlike the tower of babel, which as it grows the
people involved cannot communicate with each other. However, Armin said
this is no problem, for the LLM which is generating the code itself
provides the solution: instead of you, the human, deigning to understand
the codebase, you eventually come to rely on the AI to explain something
when you need it explained. And so it is no problem that we stop
communicating with each other, that humans become less involved with the
process: the tower keeps rising, and when you need to understand
something, you ask the LLM-AI based agent instead.

This was from a *proponent*, mind you.

So the main difference between my blogpost describing the "vibe bobsled"
and Armin's is that Armin is a proponent, and described this as upward
growth. But myself, being worried about communities and the individual
of people to communicate, describe it as downward movement.

In both cases, Armin and I do agree on something: that codebases which
use these things become incomprehensible to people, who come to rely on
AI agents to instead take over. It's merely whether you consider that
upward progress or downward decline that we disagree on.

 - Christine

Anyone who knows something about Emacs development and maintenance for
the past decade or two can immediately see that the projects described
in that blog are very different from what happens in Emacs nowadays.
While the dangers described there are not unimaginable in Emacs, there
are several factors that make them highly improbable.  One of them,
perhaps the most important one, is that Emacs's codebase is very old
and very stable, and that significantly affects the kinds of changes
are being submitted most of the time, in ways that make those dangers
much less likely to happen here.  If you carefully read what's
described in those blogs, you will clearly see that the projects and
the development activities they talk about are different in many
important aspects.

Bottom line: we should be careful when we learn from what happened in
other projects, certainly when the conclusions are so radical.

In most professional jobs I've had the quality control is the code
review. In addition to the author, who has read and written the code,

academia, which has peer review. That the test suite passes the code
is not quality control. Emacs development itself has the exact same
criteria. Here, no one has read the code.

exploits or backdoors when you haven't read it?

Phil Hagelberg <phil@hagelb.org> writes:

> Richard Stallman <rms@gnu.org> writes:
>
>> This is a rather disturbing picture.  It suggests that maintaining a
>> program whose code was generated by LLM is a complex quandry: what
>> constitutes "the source code"?  Is it the output generated by the LLM,
>> or is it the input to the LLM system?  Is either of the two really
>> usable as the source code?
>>
>> If the output, generated in some programming language, is
>> understandable as source code, and reasonable to modify,
>> that is ok.  We could designate that as "the source code".
>>
>> However, it may be difficult to edit by hand.
>
> I have worked at two different software companies where they have
> welcomed in LLM contributions, so I have firsthand experience observing
> what happens to a codebase where this is allowed. In both cases, the
> developers were very clearly instructed by management to use it
> "responsibly" and to keep the source code maintainable.
>
> The developers started out with the best intentions and initially used
> it to make edits that were reasonable in scope. But in both cases it
> didn't end there; the more they used these systems, the more comfortable
> they got with putting them in the driver's seat, and over time the
> systems decayed to the point where it was an exhausting feat to try to
> understand them.
>
> I would ask my co-workers what a function that they ostensibly wrote was
> meant to do, and I'd get blank stares back. Eventually I had to leave
> the first company (during the worst job market of my entire life) due to
> this problem.

Can you specify in what time range and using what methods (just a chat
interface, Copilot-Style completion, Agents, etc.) were employed?  My
concern is that it seems like you are jumping to general conclusions
from anecdotal evidence in a corporate setting, that doesn't seem to
warrant that any kind of LLM assistance ought to be acceptable.

If the GNU project decides to permit LLM contributions, and we follow
along, that doesn't mean we will just greenlight any LLM generated
patch.  Coming up with guidelines that ensure LLM assisted contributions
remain human-handle-able, are in line with the spirit of free software
while still allowing up to tackle issues and features that would
otherwise never find the time/attention among volunteers seems like a
much more sensible discussion to me -- which is why I again repeat my
question what examples in public, free software projects you can point
to where accepting LLM contributions had lead to real issues, so that we
can discuss what we can do better.

words for how i feel about this. what is the point of avoiding a
slippery slope if it means evil becomes acceptable? and slavery is
evil. i don't care what the law says. and i am ok with being absolutist
on this point. genocide is also evil. so is pedophilia. being born
left-handed is not, nor having red hair, nor being from russia.. life is
complicated, eli, so pick carefully what you're going to be unmovable
on, because the sequela may lead you to a dark place.

> The Free Software movement doesn't pursue the goal of "liberty for all
> humanity".  If you think it does, you are gravely mistaken.  Our goals
> are different, and are well described elsewhere.

when you wrote this, i went back and read the gnu manifesto and the
sections on philosophy at the fsf website, something i haven't done for
quite some time. i was convinced i would find something to support the
idea that the fsf's mission, while focused on software, is in support of
the greater mission of human liberty. but you are right. i was gravely
mistaken.

what i have read, instead, are a bunch of writings that use the language
of freedom and liberty to enshrine privileges for programmers and no one
else. there is no such thing as justice for only one group of people. it
must be universal. there is nothing wrong with narrowly focusing on
justice in one arena, but it must always exist in the context of the
greater, universal struggle for justice. anything else is
hypocrisy. anything else is hollow. it is morally bankrupt.

injustice anywhere is a threat to justice everywhere

i am now ashamed of my support for the fsf and gnu over the decades. i
am ashamed that i drew a meaningless distinction between free software
and open source. i am ashamed that i have defended richard stallman
because of values i thought he had, in spite of the things he has
done. i thought i owed him a debt.

in honor of richard's penchant for renaming things, i propose that we
change the =E2=80=9Cfree software foundation=E2=80=9D to the =E2=80=9Cprogr=
ammer privilege
project=E2=80=9D, or =E2=80=9Cppp=E2=80=9D for short. a protocol that was o=
nce incredible
relevant now only exists as a faded memory for old people.

i rescind my copyright assignment.

i'm fucking out.

-bjc

i do not speak for the human emacs project, i am merely a recent
signatory. i speak for myself and it is my outrage alone that is being
expressed.

On 11/6/2026 11:10 PM, Eli Zaretskii wrote:
>> Date: Fri, 6 Nov 2026 12:49:28 -0800
>> Cc: bugs@gnu.support, phil@hagelb.org, emacs-devel@gnu.org
>> From: Jim Porter <jporterbugs@gmail.com>
>>
>> Take the recent bug reports from "roelof's assistent", which
>> self-reports as an AI. [...]
> 
> Please re-read one of his bug reports and my responses, and elaborate
> why you are alarmed by what you read there.  (But please confine
> yourself to what was actually written, not to what could have been
> written in some different theoretical case.)

The issue I found most troublesome was bug#82151, which had already been 
spun off from another bug and advocated for some changes to quite tricky 
code. Message 18e3b7be1183d199.7d99f69d0b8dc578.d8d47c8e9544f598@voidpc 
in particular seemed a non sequitur to your reply and (as you noted at 
the time) didn't add anything new to the discussion. These sorts of 
things happen with human contributors as well - and I know I've been 
pushy in a bug or two on the list - but LLMs make it all the easier to 
scale up the pushiness.

Since this is but a single example, it's fair to say I'm making 
mountains out of molehills here. As mentioned though, I want to raise 
these issues while they still *are* molehills so that we're prepared. 
Had this discussion not occurred in public when it did, I might have 
preferred to just send you a short message off-list to check if those 
bugs were a bother.

I've been on the receiving end of an increasing flood of issues/patches 
of that sort in other projects, and have sadly noticed co-maintainers of 
these projects become distrustful of outsiders in proportion to the rise 
of those issues. Hopefully we can avoid that here (not just for you, but 
for anyone else who responds to bug reports).

> If you mean encouraging people to do things themselves so they learn
> better and faster, no one in their right minds will object to that.
> Nor would comments to that effect in a discussion of a submission be
> out of place, IMO.  But that is a very far cry from what the OP said
> when he started this thread, and a very-very-VERY far cry from forking
> Emacs.

That's good to hear. I think additionally making it clear that a project 
*expects* people to do things themselves to assist learning will help 
attract exactly the sort of people who want to learn and - in at least a 
few cases - step up to help maintain Emacs in the future.

These are of course only my views, since I'm just someone worried about 
the trajectory of other F/OSS projects who hopes Emacs can avoid the 
same. I don't relish forking, and view the possible fork only as a 
signpost that there will be *some* version of Emacs for those who want a 
community that prioritizes learning and developing our craft.

> This is again about those people who cannot use LLMs wisely.  It
> doesn't affect the Emacs maintainers, who need to deal with such
> attitude already, and it doesn't affect Emacs and its code.  I don't
> see why we should be responsible for people who are unwise enough to
> hurt their own abilities, and I definitely don't see how that could be
> stopped by refusing to accept LLM-generated code or by forking Emacs.

My concern is with the level of discipline needed to maintain this 
wisdom. While a few people may be able to maintain strict personal 
boundaries on how they use LLMs, their design encourages ever-greater 
adoption. (How much this is intentional, I don't know.) I'd like to 
think of myself as particularly disciplined, but I've seen enough cases 
of others going overboard that I don't want to risk it.

Currently, Emacs has fairly strict community-set limits due to the 
copyright situation. That's done much to protect against these issues 
here, and I think it would be best to avoid relaxing these limits *even 
if* the FSF concluded that LLMs don't undermine copyleft.

> I see it as a greatly exaggerated reaction to problems that are
> largely if not completely unrelated to Emacs and its development.
> Where they could be relevant, they didn't yet happen, and the fears
> (at least those I've seen written so far) are based on basic mistrust
> of our abilities and intentions as Emacs maintainers.

I don't mean this as a criticism of any of the maintainers' abilities or 
intentions (past or present). Rather, I fear that relaxing our LLM 
policies will make it harder for maintainers to apply their (our?) 
abilities and intentions to keeping Emacs on the same positive road it's 
been on for so long.

Put another way: I think our existing policies and maintainership have 
been very good. I'm suggesting that we extend the reasoning for our ban 
on LLM contributions from the temporary copyleft dispute to include 
protecting against the negative social effects seen in other projects. 
That's all, really.

In particular, I'm not suggesting Emacs immediately adopt any new 
policies. While I'm concerned about the LLM-assisted bug reports, 
they're certainly not a crisis yet, so there's no need to rush to make a 
change. For that case, all I hope for is that people on Debbugs keep in 
mind that have to deal with LLM bug spam, so we should stay alert in 
case that happens here.

> From: brian cully <bjc@spork.org>
> Cc: jporterbugs@gmail.com,  bugs@gnu.support,  phil@hagelb.org,
>   emacs-devel@gnu.org
> Date: Sat, 07 Nov 2026 20:03:52 -0500
> 
> Eli Zaretskii <eliz@gnu.org> writes:
> 
> >> as a hypothetical example: if i live in a territory that permits
> >> slavery, and by law i am granted sole ownership of the products of that
> >> forced labor, and then i use that to create contributions to gnu emacs,
> >> complete with copyright assignment, and it is technically correct, and,
> >> above all, you, the emacs maintainers are aware of how this was
> >> produced, would it be ethical to accept those contributions?
> >
> > Our answer must be YES.
> >
> > Any other answer is a first step towards splitting our community along
> > the many lines of political and ideological divides that have nothing
> > to do with software freedoms.  Right now we have contributors from all
> > over the world, despite the differences in their regimes and political
> > systems, differences in ideologies, and even in the very
> > interpretation of the notion of "freedom".  You are suggesting to
> > subject the contributors to some examination of the principles they
> > uphold, the ethics of their day-to-day activities, their views on
> > matters of policies and important international events, etc.  This
> > will immediately fracture our community into many different enclaves.
> > And that's exactly my point, and the main reason why I must reject the
> > "Human Emacs" initiative, as it is presented to us.
> 
> you have called this a “slippery slope,” that is a thought terminating
> cliche. provenance can absolutely matter, which is why i chose such a
> shocking example. i anticipated many possible replies from you, but i
> did not anticipate this one. i am shocked to the core.
> 
> you have said that you will exercise constant vigilance and yet you have
> utterly failed an incredibly simple test because you have eschewed that
> vigilance for some abstract, absolutist principle.
> 
> ironically, your avoidance of slippery slopes has led you directly into
> tolerating slavery for the benefit of gnu emacs.

No, I don't tolerate slavery.  I just don't ask our contributors how
they feel about slavery, or about any other injustices.  Because if we
start asking them, we will be bogged in questions of what exactly is
slavery and what is genocide and what are all the other injustices.
And that is a death blow to our movement.

IOW, you incorrectly conflate what we do when we accept and judge and
review contributions with our personal views on unrelated (though
important) subjects and in particular on the ethics and morals of the
contributors.

> injustice anywhere is a threat to justice everywhere

That's true, but people rarely agree what is injustice nowadays.
Someone's terrorist is another one's freedom fighter.  Someone's
justified war is another's genocide.  Etc. etc.  If we start down that
road, we end up as fragmented and fractioned as the current societies
and countries.  We will never agree on anything.  Because why should
you accept my judgment on these issues, and why should I accept yours?

> i do not speak for the human emacs project, i am merely a recent
> signatory. i speak for myself and it is my outrage alone that is being
> expressed.

Unfortunately, I suspect that quite a few of the signatories share
your views, although perhaps not all of them have thought that out to
the logical conclusion.  Which is why I made a point of pointing these
aspects explicitly, as they are at the core of my deep disagreement
with this initiative.

> >> Take the recent bug reports from "roelof's assistent", which
> >> self-reports as an AI. [...]
> > 
> > Please re-read one of his bug reports and my responses, and elaborate
> > why you are alarmed by what you read there.  (But please confine
> > yourself to what was actually written, not to what could have been
> > written in some different theoretical case.)
> 
> The issue I found most troublesome was bug#82151, which had already been 
> spun off from another bug and advocated for some changes to quite tricky 
> code. Message 18e3b7be1183d199.7d99f69d0b8dc578.d8d47c8e9544f598@voidpc 
> in particular seemed a non sequitur to your reply and (as you noted at 
> the time) didn't add anything new to the discussion. These sorts of 
> things happen with human contributors as well - and I know I've been 
> pushy in a bug or two on the list - but LLMs make it all the easier to 
> scale up the pushiness.

Why do you find this troublesome?  Do you think I handled those
messages incorrectly or badly?  What I did was to take the ideas of
the message, check them against the code I'm familiar with, and
respond with critique and/or requests for more info.  Isn't that what
we as maintainers are supposed to do when presented with bug reports
accompanied by potential explanations?

> Since this is but a single example, it's fair to say I'm making 
> mountains out of molehills here.

TBH, I fail to see the mountain.  When we receive a bug report which
describes a segfault with a backtrace, we must investigate, don't we?
And investigating means considering every idea about the possible
causes of the segfault, doesn't it?  So why are you alarmed by that
discussion, out of all the other similar discussions we have on the
bug tracker?

> As mentioned though, I want to raise 
> these issues while they still *are* molehills so that we're prepared. 

Prepared to what, exactly?

> Had this discussion not occurred in public when it did, I might have 
> preferred to just send you a short message off-list to check if those 
> bugs were a bother.

How can a report about a segfault NOT be a bother?  But if you mean
the information provided by the reporter, then no, it wasn't a bother,
no more than a similar report from anyone else would be.  The ability
to quickly scan a report and see its main points is again part of our
job.

> I've been on the receiving end of an increasing flood of issues/patches 
> of that sort in other projects, and have sadly noticed co-maintainers of 
> these projects become distrustful of outsiders in proportion to the rise 
> of those issues. Hopefully we can avoid that here (not just for you, but 
> for anyone else who responds to bug reports).

Do you see any signs or indications of that happening here?  If so,
can you point them out?

And what do you mean by "flood"?  If we will get a flood of reports
about different segfaults, we would be very surprised, I think, but
segfaults must be investigated.  What else can we do?

And if we are flooded with reports about minor or non-existing issues,
we should be able to filter them out efficiently, as we did until now.
So what is the nature of your worries here?

> > If you mean encouraging people to do things themselves so they learn
> > better and faster, no one in their right minds will object to that.
> > Nor would comments to that effect in a discussion of a submission be
> > out of place, IMO.  But that is a very far cry from what the OP said
> > when he started this thread, and a very-very-VERY far cry from forking
> > Emacs.
> 
> That's good to hear. I think additionally making it clear that a project 
> *expects* people to do things themselves to assist learning will help 
> attract exactly the sort of people who want to learn and - in at least a 
> few cases - step up to help maintain Emacs in the future.

The project doesn't expect anything.  We are not a nursery.  We treat
our contributors as grownups and expect them to behave accordingly.
We offer support for what we consider to be useful for their future
contributions, but we cannot be held responsible for being their
nannies.

> These are of course only my views, since I'm just someone worried about 
> the trajectory of other F/OSS projects who hopes Emacs can avoid the 
> same. I don't relish forking, and view the possible fork only as a 
> signpost that there will be *some* version of Emacs for those who want a 
> community that prioritizes learning and developing our craft.

What does this have to do with LLM-generated code, though?

> > This is again about those people who cannot use LLMs wisely.  It
> > doesn't affect the Emacs maintainers, who need to deal with such
> > attitude already, and it doesn't affect Emacs and its code.  I don't
> > see why we should be responsible for people who are unwise enough to
> > hurt their own abilities, and I definitely don't see how that could be
> > stopped by refusing to accept LLM-generated code or by forking Emacs.
> 
> My concern is with the level of discipline needed to maintain this 
> wisdom. While a few people may be able to maintain strict personal 
> boundaries on how they use LLMs, their design encourages ever-greater 
> adoption. (How much this is intentional, I don't know.) I'd like to 
> think of myself as particularly disciplined, but I've seen enough cases 
> of others going overboard that I don't want to risk it.
> 
> Currently, Emacs has fairly strict community-set limits due to the 
> copyright situation. That's done much to protect against these issues 
> here, and I think it would be best to avoid relaxing these limits *even 
> if* the FSF concluded that LLMs don't undermine copyleft.

You cannot protect people from themselves, not by these measures.  And
it is not our place nor our job to do that.

> > I see it as a greatly exaggerated reaction to problems that are
> > largely if not completely unrelated to Emacs and its development.
> > Where they could be relevant, they didn't yet happen, and the fears
> > (at least those I've seen written so far) are based on basic mistrust
> > of our abilities and intentions as Emacs maintainers.
> 
> I don't mean this as a criticism of any of the maintainers' abilities or 
> intentions (past or present). Rather, I fear that relaxing our LLM 
> policies will make it harder for maintainers to apply their (our?) 
> abilities and intentions to keeping Emacs on the same positive road it's 
> been on for so long.

There are many factors that make our job harder when they happen.  We
deal with them.  I see no reason to believe we will be unable to deal
with this one as well.

> Put another way: I think our existing policies and maintainership have 
> been very good. I'm suggesting that we extend the reasoning for our ban 
> on LLM contributions from the temporary copyleft dispute to include 
> protecting against the negative social effects seen in other projects. 
> That's all, really.

I see no signs we need any extra protection of these sorts.  All I see
is unfounded fears of something that didn't happen.  Dealing with
people who post nonsense and worse is something we do all the time,
and having that come from LLM doesn't change it.

> In particular, I'm not suggesting Emacs immediately adopt any new 
> policies. While I'm concerned about the LLM-assisted bug reports, 
> they're certainly not a crisis yet, so there's no need to rush to make a 
> change. For that case, all I hope for is that people on Debbugs keep in 
> mind that have to deal with LLM bug spam, so we should stay alert in 
> case that happens here.

Then there's no need for the "Human Emacs" initiative yet, not until
and unless there are clear signs of deterioration in the quality of
our code, the ability of the maintainers to do their job correctly,
and any other adverse effects on our conduct and exchange on our
forums.

Just to answer to above with the quote from:
https://www.gnu.org/philosophy/kind-communication.html

Please don't raise unrelated political issues in GNU Project 
discussions, because they are off-topic. The only political positions 
that the GNU Project endorses are (1) that users should have control of 
their own computing (for instance, through free software) and (2) 
supporting basic human rights in computing. We don't require you as a 
contributor to agree with these two points, but you do need to accept 
that our decisions will be based on them.

That is why we are all participants and users of GNU project, no matter 
the other politics. We are here discussing, creating, and using the free 
software and freedom in computing.

What Eli answered to you, it was kind and enlightening, and in the 
spirit of the GNU project, and principles already explained keep the GNU 
project running.

> ironically, your avoidance of slippery slopes has led you directly into
> tolerating slavery for the benefit of gnu emacs.

society as slavery is alright, though GNU project doesn't deal with 
those.

SaaSS of any kind, not just LLM, that it subjugates users and users give

Joel Reicher <joel.reicher@gmail.com> writes:

> Richard Stallman <rms@gnu.org> writes:
>
>> [[[ To any NSA and FBI agents reading my email: please consider ]]]
>> [[[ whether defending the US Constitution against all enemies, ]]]
>> [[[ foreign or domestic, requires you to follow Snowden's
>> example. ]]]
>>
>> Aside from platform-specific low-level adaptations, it must be
>> possible to build Emacs from source using free software.
>>
>> In order for this to include converting C++ code to Elisp code using
>> an LLM, it needs to use a free LLM.

Why?  I understand the concern if we are talking about tools that
interface with LLMs, but as for the translation itself it doesn't seem
to matter how it was done.  It seems to me to be the same concern as if
someone wrote the package using a non-free text editor or had it written
by someone who didn't publish it under a free license, but then sells
the rights to someone who publish it under a free license.

> My main concern with this approach is whether it's a reproducible
> build. A different LLM (or different model) might yield
> semantically-significant different results, unlike a multitude of
> valid compilers where validity implies a kind of semantic equivalence.

The translation is not part of the build-process.  To use the package,
you yourself don't have use any LLM again.  But yes, if you were to
translate it again, the result would presumably differ (unless you used
some method to make the LLM deterministic) just as it would differ if
you had a human translate the code.

> Thanks and regards,
>
>       - Joel

This very much depends on what one considers the "preferred form" in
GNU parlance. Richard seems to tend to (a) the original C++ (in that
case you'd need the whole build tooling plus the build parameters),
whereas you seem to tend (b) towards the generated Lisp.

Both standpoints seem possible. In practical terms, it seems to me
that in case (b), it is just a starting point, and further modifications
happen on the (originally generated) Lisp code. Fixes to the C++
code would have to be ported (by hand? with yet another LLM?) to
the Lisp code. Whatever is needed for this maintenance work should
be feasible with free tools, right?

Cheers

Hello everyone,

The first pretest for what will be the 31.1 release of Emacs (the
extensible text editor) is now available at:

  https://alpha.gnu.org/gnu/emacs/pretest/emacs-31.1.91.tar.xz

The tarball is signed; you can get the PGP signature file at:

  https://alpha.gnu.org/gnu/emacs/pretest/emacs-31.1.91.tar.xz.sig

Please give it as much testing as you can.

As always, if you encounter problems building or using Emacs,
send a report to bug-gnu-emacs@gnu.org with full details
(if possible, use M-x report-emacs-bug).

Thanks for helping to test Emacs.

=2D-------------------------------------

To verify that the tarball is intact, download both the .sig and
the tarball, and run this command:

  gpg --verify emacs-31.1.91.tar.xz.sig

If that command fails because you don't have the required public key,
run this command to import it:

  gpg --keyserver keyring.debian.org --recv-keys \
    8DC2487E51ABDD90B5C4753F0F56D0553B6D411B

You can also run sha256sum or sha512sum and confirm that these checksums
match:

SHA256  emacs-31.1.91.tar.xz
ABAC96A397DE99C5F8419C02F9343A672D9B144AC90E9CFD0399472647D7B5FA

SHA512  emacs-31.1.91.tar.xz
379613A9B8DAF05C748CBC3E5D1317777F110CEA4F42363DE4C324BE45C6BFE8E4277EA02BF=
112F016EF660695F1D0CC6012E0C908A3F359AD22A98BD0ADE31C

=2D---------------------------------------

For a summary of changes in Emacs 31, see the etc/NEWS file in the
tarball; you can view it from Emacs by typing 'C-h n', or by clicking
Help->Emacs News from the menu bar.

You can also browse NEWS on-line using this URL:

  https://git.savannah.gnu.org/cgit/emacs.git/tree/etc/NEWS?h=3Demacs-31

For the complete list of changes and the people who made them, see the
various ChangeLog files in the source distribution.  For a summary of
all the people who have contributed to Emacs, see the etc/AUTHORS
file.

For more information about Emacs, see:
  https://www.gnu.org/software/emacs

=2D-=20
Sean Whitton

On 07/11/2026 09:37, Eli Zaretskii wrote:
> Forking is different, at least potentially, because it completely
> severs the relation to the original code, and that original code is
> not needed to make subsequent changes.

I won't know, seems similar enough as a question. Many known forks have 
been applying new changes from their original projects, over the years.

> That is why I asked what would be the workflow for someone to
> "cherry-pick" an upstream change in Hunspell into vibe-spell.  The
> answer should tell us whether the original source is important or not.

You start the agent in the new project's dir, point it to the "original" 
project's dir, and tell it to apply or adopt the change with commit 
so-and-so. That should work.

If we want to exclude the previous project and just pass the commit's 
diff, that should also generally work, but I suppose the number of edge 
cases when it fails, would be higher.

Anyway, just using the patches from the original project would likely 
succeed, but that also depends on how much the new project's 
architecture had been altered in the rewrite (not just the language used).

> > Then there's no need for the "Human Emacs" initiative yet, not until

> Why this degree of deliberate blindness, Eli? There have been empirical
> studies for years about the adverse effects of LLMs on code quality ([0],
> [1]).

As already explained, it is the job of the Emacs maintainers to keep
the code quality high and not allow any low-quality code into Emacs.
We are doing that every day, regardless of the source of the code.
The message that you quote says that until there are signs that we the
maintainers are unable to do this job, there's no need for any
preventive measures on that account.

So what I wrote and you quoted has nothing to do with the studies
about quality of LLM-generated code.

> Moreover, why is the initiative of Human Emacs being presented in so
> negative light? That it is a threat, that it wants to split the community,
> etc.

Because that's what the words I read tell me.  "Do something or else".

> As a signatory to the initiative, I urge people here to please consider this a
> plea in good faith by people who have loved and contributed to GNU Emacs for
> years but are worried about it being coopted into the same path that has led
> others into eventually prioritizing this technology's usage over their own
> contributors.

I never intended to say that there's any bad faith, and I don't think
so.  I just disagree with the premise and the conclusions.

> The reference here is to the Linux Kernel project:
> 
> > Torvalds answered that the kernel project only wants serious developers.
> That includes having access to enough resources to function in this world.
> 
> https://lwn.net/Articles/1099594/
> 
> Why this is not alarming to Emacs maintainers is really a surprise to me.

It is not alarming because Emacs is not the Linux kernel, and there's
no reason to assume we will make the same decisions as Torvalds
allegedly/reportedly made.

> This technology's relationship to copyright, free software and
> other things has been of nothing but destructive. It has been used
> to launder (L)GPL'ed projects [2].

The copyright issues are looked into by the lawyers, and we await the
GNU decisions following what the lawyers recommend.  As for the rest,
the fact that other projects made mistakes doesn't mean we will make
them here.

> Many other big projects like Codeberg and Zig have rejected it for these
> destructive aspects. Why are we being so defensive as to not even opening a
> proper dialogue about it without accusations of splitting the community?

This thread _is_ a dialog.

As for accusations, I don't agree that I accused anyone, no more than
the original message was an accusation aimed at the Emacs project.  I
disagree, yes, but disagreement is not an accusation.  I said that a
fork will split the community, but that's not an accusation, either,
it's a simple self-evident consequence of a fork.

> You know who has been already splitting the community? People just using these
> LLMs to clone existing Emacs packages instead of contributing to them. Forks
> like Neomacs that have no intention of helping Emacs. Human Emacs is precisely
> on the side of community, because this LLM technology rejects one of the
> fundamental ideas that motivated Free Software: growing together as a
> community.

What does this have to do with the issue at hand?  No one here is
involved in Neomacs, and I hope you are not saying that the Emacs
maintainers have no intention of helping Emacs.

> To quote from the GNU Manifesto [3]:
> 
> > I consider that the Golden Rule requires that if I like a program I must
> share it with other people who like it. Software sellers want to divide the
> users and conquer them, making each user agree not to share with others.
> 
> The spirit that this technology has been embodying since it's inception has
> been closer to Open Source than Free Software. It says: "who cares about
> learning and collaborating with existing software/humans, let's just pay a bit
> more and write our own". This is not what we want, if we were to follow the
> Golden Rule.

Rest assured, we are not going to change our support for sharing
software, nor will we give up any other principle of Free Software.
It doesn't matter what others do or say, we will not change our
principles, regardless of the way the code we accept was written.

> GNU was built by and for hackers, and the hacker spirit is to collaborate,
> share and grow together. LLM ideology pushes one to forget anything related to
> any of those values, be individualist and just focus on supposed technological
> improvement. This was what Open Source did, not Free Software.

The free software movement, and the Emacs project in particular, don't
care about ideology of those who contribute to our projects.  We care
about the code being well designed and well implemented, and we care
for it to be free.  No ideology of anyone can affect those standards
of ours.

> So, yes of course we have to think about what kinds of social imperatives we
> are espousing when we take one decision or another. This is what should be
> discussed, and this is what we are requesting for, to take us as enemies who
> want to just fork is to not take us seriously.

Accepting code generated this or that way does not espouse any
ideology or social imperative.  Your mistake is that you think there's
some link between accepting code from a person and upholding the
principles, views, and ethics of that person.  There's no link, and
should not be any such link, for the reasons I explained: if we start
examining these aspects, we will immediately split our community,
because there are many issues on which we don't agree.

> RMS has also given examples elsewhere of how it's important to understand what
> kind of incentives we're rewarding that benefits the society or not.
> 
> Earlier in the thread you nodded to accepting code that is a product of
> slavery, what are we incentivizing? What about child slavery? We are okay with
> not wondering if we are effevtively incentivizing the exploitation of
> children? 

Are you okay with accepting code from countries whose policies you
condemn or whose regimes you consider cruel and inhuman?  If yes, why
is that different from the slavery example above?  And if you think
we should reject code from such countries, then where does it stop?

> I understand these are difficult questions and we can't answer them
> immediately, but to absolutely ignore these questions is against the spirit of
> Free Software, in my opinion.

I don't ignore these questions, not at all.  I just have answers that
you disagree with.  And that's okay, because we should be able to work
on improving Emacs regardless of our differences on those other
issues.  By working on Emacs we make contribution to the goodness of
the society in one particular aspect: software freedom.

> If we were worried about 'splitting' why did we
> emphasizing social imperative and philosophy against Open Source? We could've
> just said: "oh well, if TiVo wants to close it down, it's upto them, we can't
> fight these battles." Of course we can. Similarly this LLM technology has many
> aspects about how they harm free software and the users, and the society at
> large. These are valid questions that need to be discussed. If we want to
> throw these questions off the window, we might as well stop being Free
> Software and say we're just concerned with imoroving technology and accepting
> code patches regardless of how they're made like the Open Source people have
> been and are saying.

You are conflating unrelated issues here.  In particular, the place of
discussing issues unrelated to software freedom is not here.

> We have to remember what GNU stood for, a revolt against properietary
> technology, against a society where freedom in computing is infringed. LLMs
> are a risk to this freedom too, and as such GNU cannot just embrace it with
> open arms like the Linux Foundation did. I urge people to please think
> critically about this and not take Human Emacs as a threat, but as a
> plea/request to preserve the spirit of Free Software and GNU Emacs.

I don't see why LLMs are a risk so high that we must completely reject
it.  We should mitigate the risks, as we do with any other risks.  So
far I see no reason why our existing mitigation methods should fail to
work, but if we find in the future that some changes in our procedures
are needed, we will at that time make the necessary changes.

Divya Ranjan Pattanaik <divya@dialetheia.xyz> writes:

>> Then there's no need for the "Human Emacs" initiative yet, not until
>> and unless there are clear signs of deterioration in the quality of
>> our code, the ability of the maintainers to do their job correctly,
>> and any other adverse effects on our conduct and exchange on our
>> forums.
>
> Why this degree of deliberate blindness, Eli? There have been
> empirical studies for years about the adverse effects of LLMs on code
> quality ([0], [1]).  Moreover, why is the initiative of Human Emacs
> being presented in so negative light? That it is a threat, that it
> wants to split the community, etc.

It is worth noting that both of these studies are over a year old
(November '24, February '25) and that much has changed since then.  My
impression is that a large part of the problem in this discussion is
that it feels like those advocating against LLMs /in general/ are doing
so because they have decided that that is the point they want to take
and are looking for arguments to substantiate that position.  To give a
silly analogy, it feels like a discussion where one side is trying to
make a general claim against trains by specifically talking about steam
engines.  I am not asking you to agree with the analogy, I am just
trying to illustrate a one reason why people can be skeptical of the
claims of the "Human Emacs" initiative and why this can be exhausting.

But more seriously, and I have tried to raise this point in the thread
before, if the GNU project decides to decide allow LLM contributions the
Emacs maintainers don't only have the two options that the "Human Emacs"
initiative argues ("Yes, everything is allowed" or "No, nothing is
allowed") but there is a spectrum in between.  I still think, and this
is perhaps even more relevant for ELPA than for the more conservative
Emacs codebase, that spelling out under what conditions LLM generated
code stands in contradiction to the values of software freedom and
trying to do our best to enforce these would be more productive.

My disappointment is the "Human Emacs" initiative is that they want to
entirely sidestep this discussion with an entirely abstention-ist
position that under no circumstances, any kind of LLM assisted
contributions are acceptable seems to be on the face of it an absurdly
strong statement that I don't think that be substantiated.  I would urge
the people behind the initiative to, as a sign of good will, take down
their "Not Under Discussion" section from the website because that is
essentially what the discussion is about.

> As a signatory to the initiative, I urge people here to please
> consider this a plea in good faith by people who have loved and
> contributed to GNU Emacs for years but are worried about it being
> coopted into the same path that has led others into eventually
> prioritizing this technology's usage over their own contributors. The
> reference here is to the Linux Kernel project:
>
>> Torvalds answered that the kernel project only wants serious developers. That includes having access to enough resources to function in this world.
>
> https://lwn.net/Articles/1099594/
>
> Why this is not alarming to Emacs maintainers is really a surprise to
> me. This technology's relationship to copyright, free software and
> other things has been of nothing but destructive. It has been used to
> launder (L)GPL'ed projects [2].

This is a point that I do not find convincing, unless you want to
believe in the conclusion.  Yes, LLMs can be used to endanger software
freedom, but the missing argument is to show why this is an inherent
issue of LLMs.  A human can Emacs itself can be used to launder a
stronger copyleft license by writing a more permissive alternative, or
even non-free software.  But just like how perhaps even by default
computers are coercive, conservative and oppressive instruments in
society (which makes sense considering the effort and interests in
developing these machines), this can be subverted by free software into
creating liberatory tools that enhance human agency -- the potential for
both is there.  And that is just like how the free software movement,
which is essentially for better or worse a legalistic initiative,
subverts copyright law (which again, by default would restrict the user
from actualizing the positive potential of software) into a means to
actually protect and subsist free software within the existing system, I
think that in the context of LLMs we ought to be considering how we can
"hack" the system into helping us serve our goals instead of undermining
them.

But back to the concrete issues, can you or anyone else who has signed
onto the initiative explain what the problem is with allowing LLM
contributions under a strict guideline.  Take the Ghostty project for
instance, who have a AI_POLICY.md file [0] that for instance require

  [...]

  - **The human-in-the-loop must fully understand all code.** If you
    can't explain what your changes do and how they interact with the
    greater system without the aid of AI tools, do not contribute
    to this project.

  - **Issues and discussions can use AI assistance but must have a full
    human-in-the-loop.** This means that any content generated with AI
    must have been reviewed _and edited_ by a human before submission.
    AI is very good at being overly verbose and including noise that
    distracts from the main point. Humans must do their research and
    trim this down.

  [...]

[0] https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ghostty-org/ghostty/refs/heads/main/AI_POLICY.md

> Many other big projects like Codeberg and Zig have rejected it for
> these destructive aspects. Why are we being so defensive as to not
> even opening a proper dialogue about it without accusations of
> splitting the community?

Please correct me if I am mistaken, but considering what I have written
above, the impression I get is that the "Human Emacs" initiative are not
interested in a proper dialogue, since the position is tantamount to
them asserting "agree with our fixed points, or we fork -- there are no
other options".

> You know who has been already splitting the community? People just
> using these LLMs to clone existing Emacs packages instead of
> contributing to them. Forks like Neomacs that have no intention of
> helping Emacs. Human Emacs is precisely on the side of community,
> because this LLM technology rejects one of the fundamental ideas that
> motivated Free Software: growing together as a community. 

It is not that relevant to the discussion at hand, but I still want to
point out that it is entirely consistent with the values of free
software to make changes locally and not share them publicly.  You are
expected to share the source in a usable way if you want to share the
changes to someone else, but that doesn't mean that you have to upstream
everything to the global community.  I do understand that this is to a
certain degree regrettable, but I think that within software freedom
advocacy there is some leeway here since an LLM can help some people
actualize their freedom to make local changes to the software they use,
which they otherwise wouldn't be in a position to due to time or
knowledge restraints.

>                                                           To quote
> from the GNU Manifesto [3]:
>
>> I consider that the Golden Rule requires that if I like a program I
>> must share it with other people who like it. Software sellers want to
>> divide the users and conquer them, making each user agree not to
>> share with others.
>
> The spirit that this technology has been embodying since it's
> inception has been closer to Open Source than Free Software. It says:

>

>

(I don't have much more to add to the remainder of these points, but if
you do think I skipped over something that relates to my comments from

I just want to for my own sake clarify that I do sympathize with these
points.  I know that you, as well as most others that have signed the

we agree on core principles.

Sorry to barge in as an outsider, but these two points confused me and 
seem relevant to GNU as a whole:

 > Eli Zaretskii <eliz@gnu.org> wrote:
 > So basically, you are saying that just because LLMs can and perhaps do
 > harm elsewhere, we should not let them anywhere near Emacs, regardless
 > of what they can or cannot do to Emacs and our community.
 > [...]
 > Any other answer is a first step towards splitting our community along
 > the many lines of political and ideological divides that have nothing
 > to do with software freedoms.

I would like to express my confusion why this is being discussed like a 
politics issue rather than a code of conduct issue,

The argument I quoted baffled me because since with the same line of 
reasoning, I feel like one could decline any sort of Code of Conduct as 
too radical and that it would split communities.


Now I understand that on some level this would make sense, if it really 
wasn't relevant to the project itself, but that feels arguably untrue:

1. The copyright questions seem to continue to be unresolved, even for 
some small snippets: 
https://fsfe.org/news/2026/news-20260825-01.en.html (I'm not a lawyer so 
I can't judge this for myself, but I'd like to additionally express my 
confusion why this article doesn't conclude "it seems best for projects 
to not touch this tech for now"..)

2. It seems like AI can real harm on its users. Now you might argue you 
can avoid it personally, but can everyone? You could say its the 
responsibility of every contributor, but that may not always work out, 
so I think a risk for the project itself is undeniable, even if low.

3. Higher risk for long term maintenance also seem pretty clear, since 
human reviews apparently often can't keep up with the amount of code LLM 
contributors produce.

4. I saw elsewhere the comparison you don't ask if contributors support 
slave labor in other ventures. But surely that's a bit different from 
allowing some form of slave labor product to directly knowingly 
contribute to your project. (Not just people who have that view, but a 
product, often proprietary, that has this known association, directly 
altering the code base.) I feel like that's a more direct impact worth 
considering on a local project level.


Now I'm not saying the logical conclusion is an LLM ban.[1]

I just don't get these arguments that it is naturally out of scope.

And downstream users can still do with the code whatever they want, 
including using LLMs with it, so this doesn't feel very restrictive.

I think an additional thing to consider here is that any choice, 
including no AI policy or a lenient policy, may also split the 
community, maybe even worse so.

My apologies if I'm simply misunderstanding something here.

[1]: I won't hide that I personally think that is the logical 
conclusion. But that's really besides the point of my inquiry.

Regards,

Ellie

PS: My apologies if this doesn't show up as a reply to 
https://lists.gnu.org/archive/html/emacs-devel/2026-11/msg00128.html as 
I intended. It's not entirely clear to me if Thunderbird supports 
carrying over the "Reply-To" header from the mail archive's reply button.

Stefan Monnier <monnier@iro.umontreal.ca> writes:

> Hi,
>
>>     Add heuristic for VC packages to avoid duplicate dependencies
>>     
>>     * lisp/emacs-lisp/package-vc.el (package-vc--unpack-1): Assume every
>>     basename of all files in :lisp-dir might be packages and remove them
>>     from the list of dependencies to install.  (Bug#81908)
>
> After reading Bug#81908, I still don't quite understand what this patch
> intends to avoid and how it works.  I understand that the `dash` package
> might be a concrete case, tho maybe it needs its `dash-functional` "subpackage"
> thrown into the mix, but it's still fairly fuzzy.  Could you describe
> the shape of the problem in more detail?

If packages foo and bar, where bar depends on foo are developed within
the same repository, installing foo using package-vc would scan the
repository for Package-Requires headers and find that bar depends on foo
(the package being installed).  The consequence therefore would be that
we would install foo, the tarball, before installing foo, the VC
package, and end up in a situation with both of these packages
installed.

I hope that makes sense?  Dan, please correct me if I misremembered.

https://www.gnu.org/gnu/manifesto.html

The Manifesto is not contradicted by machine-generated code. It is 
contradicted by machine-generated code that arrives without the four 
freedoms attached — and by the corporate arrangement that turns a shared 
body of programmers' work into a closed service.

Using a SaaSS LLM, non-free inference software, non-free drivers or 
firmware blobs, or an LLM trained on non-free data strips users of the 
four freedoms, because the code they receive carries no freedom with it.

On 2026-11-08 16:47, Divya Ranjan Pattanaik wrote:
> Why this degree of deliberate blindness, Eli? There have been
> empirical studies for years about the adverse effects of LLMs on code
> quality ([0], [1]). Moreover, why is the initiative of Human Emacs
> being presented in so negative light? That it is a threat, that it
> wants to split the community, etc.

I see no deliberate blindness from Eli, I just see careful consideration 
and choices based on GNU project purposes and GNU free software 
philosophy.

As it says here: https://www.gnu.org/philosophy/kind-communication.html  
"The only political positions that the GNU Project endorses are (1) that 
users should have control of their own computing (for instance, through 
free software) and (2) supporting basic human rights in computing" -- 
and so decisions are made based on that.

And there you have the emerging group of people signing up to fork the 
Emacs and many of them not knowing consequences of supporting their 
leader.

And you have the GNU project, which many of those signatories are part 
of anyway.

The "Human" Emacs group has different politics than GNU project, they 
are Anti-AI, different politics.

They are not signing really because of the fork. Majority of them are 
signing because they see injustice with the LLMs. And majority is also 
oblivious to consequences of the fork.

They are also manipulated by their leader, by telling people more of the 
subject A (negativity of LLMs), to get the apparent consent of the 
subject B (splitting community by making the fork). The "Human" mailing 
list shows that majority of people who "sign" the "Human" Emacs 
manifesto, did not discuss anything about the fork, or GNU project, or 
consequences of it.

> Why this is not alarming to Emacs maintainers is really a surprise to
> me. This technology's relationship to copyright, free software and
> other things has been of nothing but destructive. It has been used to
> launder (L)GPL'ed projects [2].

That may well be true, and I am sure the Emacs and GNU maintainers are 
gaining awareness of it. But generalization does not help. In 
engineering, what matters is not the generalization but the practical 
details. A scaffold loses its stability when built from a general idea; 
it holds when built from the specific details of the fabrication. The 
devil is in the details.

> Many other big projects like Codeberg and Zig have rejected it for
> these destructive aspects. Why are we being so defensive as to not
> even opening a proper dialogue about it without accusations of
> splitting the community?

Codeberg is not the GNU Project, and it has its own political positions, 
so its decisions do not define the terms of GNU discussion. The only 
positions the GNU Project endorses are users' control of their own 
computing and basic human rights in computing, and its decisions are 
based on those.

As for dialogue: the "Human" Emacs initiative was not a dialogue. It was 
essentially a one-person project, and most signatories were recruited on 
a subject they did not understand, not on the fork itself.

What is happening now — through your outreach and that of others — is 
the proper dialogue. That is the right way to handle it, and it is worth 
continuing rather than relitigating the earlier approach.

> You know who has been already splitting the community? People just
> using these LLMs to clone existing Emacs packages instead of
> contributing to them. Forks like Neomacs that have no intention of
> helping Emacs. Human Emacs is precisely on the side of community,
> because this LLM technology rejects one of the fundamental ideas that
> motivated Free Software: growing together as a community. To quote
> from the GNU Manifesto [3]:
> 
>> I consider that the Golden Rule requires that if I like a program I
> must share it with other people who like it. Software sellers want to
> divide the users and conquer them, making each user agree not to share
> with others.

To your above statements:

- cloning the package under the GPL does not make anyone agree not to 
share. Your analogy does not fit.

- forking is sharing. The Manifesto says everyone will be permitted to 
modify and redistribute, and that the fundamental act of friendship 
among programmers is the sharing of programs. A fork that keeps the 
license intact is the Golden Rule in action, not a violation of it.

- Contribution is a freedom, not a duty. Making and distributing copies 
is explicitly not an obligation. "Instead of contributing to them" 
assumes a duty that free software does not impose.

And I do not see how Neomacs divides community, as they do not speak of 
any radical politics to reject X, or otherwise will be consequence Y -- 
they made a fork, and shared it with the world. Great thing. If the 
feature of "fully threaded Emacs" would really work well, and Emacs 
maintainers can study it, such a feature could be implemented in Emacs. 
By sharing the software, they have already contributed back.

The only problem is in copyrights, and in that case the software can be 
re-written to be used.

When "Human" Emacs forks -- that means copyrights will not be assigned 
to the FSF, so FSF cannot easily accept such "Human" Emacs patches 
unless they are assigned to the FSF.

It implies that there may be still people contributing both to the 
"Human" Emacs and the GNU Emacs, as conscious contributors wish to share 
software for the benefit of majority of users, not just those using 
"Human" Emacs.

> The spirit that this technology has been embodying since it's
> inception has been closer to Open Source than Free Software. It says:
> "who cares about learning and collaborating with existing
> software/humans, let's just pay a bit more and write our own". This is
> not what we want, if we were to follow the Golden Rule.

Open Source camp is defined by refusing to treat the issue as justice to 
users and arguing from practical benefits only.

And the Golden Rule is about the sharing not about learning from 
existing code.

Programmers have always learned by copying: reading other people's code, 
borrowing patterns, reusing snippets. Stallman says this copying is as 
natural and as productive as breathing, and it should be free.

An LLM does the same thing, only at enormous scale. It was built by 
absorbing code that people shared, and it reproduces patterns from that 
shared body of work. So the model is not against the Manifesto's view of 
copying — it is that same act, magnified.

The model is a machine that copies at industrial scale, and copying is 
exactly what the Manifesto defends as natural, productive, and free.

Conditionally, that all the software, datasets, drivers and firmware are 
free too.

> GNU was built by and for hackers, and the hacker spirit is to
> collaborate, share and grow together. LLM ideology pushes one to
> forget anything related to any of those values, be individualist and
> just focus on supposed technological improvement. This was what Open
> Source did, not Free Software.

"LLM ideology" belongs to the companies and users, not the model. The 
Manifesto addresses agents who can choose — someone who can refuse an 
NDA, share a program, or be punished for restricting use. A model cannot 
choose, so it cannot embody a value.

Individualism is not the opposite of sharing. The opposite of sharing is 
restriction, not independence. Writing code alone and releasing it under 
the GPL is sharing.

And Open Source camp doesn't restrict sharing. Its actual flaw is amoral 
framing: it declines to see the issue as justice to users and argues 
from practical benefits only.

Technical improvement is not the enemy. Problem is when people choose 
technical improvement on technical grounds alone, when that choice means 
accepting a nonfree program.

That is my personal problem too, people talking "LLM" while they mean 
SaaSS as remote inference or non-free LLM as local inference.

> So, yes of course we have to think about what kinds of social
> imperatives we are espousing when we take one decision or another.
> This is what should be discussed, and this is what we are requesting
> for, to take us as enemies who want to just fork is to not take us
> seriously.

Definitely not enemies. Proponents of certain politics, but not enemies. 
Just that changing politics in GNU isn't going to work anyway. You could 
have read the statement on politics:

https://www.gnu.org/philosophy/kind-communication.html

Please don't raise unrelated political issues in GNU Project 
discussions, because they are off-topic. The only political positions 
that the GNU Project endorses are (1) that users should have control of 
their own computing (for instance, through free software) and (2) 
supporting basic human rights in computing. We don't require you as a 
contributor to agree with these two points, but you do need to accept 
that our decisions will be based on them.

So you see there... how decisions will be based.

> RMS has also given examples elsewhere of how it's important to
> understand what kind of incentives we're rewarding that benefits the
> society or not.

I am sure RMS has put so much thought in it, and organized other people 
to help him in identifying issues.

> Earlier in the thread you nodded to accepting code that is a product
> of slavery, what are we incentivizing? What about child slavery? We
> are okay with not wondering if we are effevtively incentivizing the
> exploitation of children?

You are missing the point. Eli was speaking hypothetically about the 
burden on maintainers. Maintainers have no time to preach or review any 
politics beyond software sharing, and the GNU Project endorses only two 
political positions: users' control of their own computing, and basic 
human rights in computing. So maintainers do not investigate political 
movements, identities, countries, or origins of contributors. They are 
simply maintainers of GNU Emacs — their mandate is the code and the 
license, not the biography behind each patch.

One is public representation, and other aspect are private opinions. I 
have no doubt that neither Eli or any other maintainer endorses child 
slavery or exploitation of children. They are naturally against it.

In science it is similar, some Nazis have invented V-2 rocketry and 
maybe those principles help people to survive moving to Mars, who knows. 
Ronald Fisher was eugenicist and he is acknowledged for statistics that 
modern science depends on. Those are bad examples, but they show that 
science also doesn't hold much of the politics.

-- 
Jean Louis

Yes.  To elaborate more about excluding base .el file names rather than
just the vc package name, I think it is for cases like this:

Repository A:

./A
=E2=94=9C=E2=94=80=E2=94=80 A-1.el      ;; Package-Requires: ((A "0"))
=E2=94=9C=E2=94=80=E2=94=80 A-2.el      ;; Package-Requires: ((A-1 "0") (B =
"0"))
=E2=94=94=E2=94=80=E2=94=80 A.el        ;; Package-Requires: ()

Where "A", "A-1", "A-2" are 3 packages on an archive.

Without excluding, installing vc "A" will end up installing tarball
packages "A", "A-1" in addition to vc "A" (B is always installed).  By
checking file names, we prevent installing tarball "A-1", better than
just excluding "A" by package names.




----Dan.

> Date: Mon, 9 Nov 2026 05:57:08 +0000
> From: Ellie <el@horse64.org>
> 
>  > Eli Zaretskii <eliz@gnu.org> wrote:
>  > So basically, you are saying that just because LLMs can and perhaps do
>  > harm elsewhere, we should not let them anywhere near Emacs, regardless
>  > of what they can or cannot do to Emacs and our community.
>  > [...]
>  > Any other answer is a first step towards splitting our community along
>  > the many lines of political and ideological divides that have nothing
>  > to do with software freedoms.
> 
> I would like to express my confusion why this is being discussed like a 
> politics issue rather than a code of conduct issue,
> 
> The argument I quoted baffled me because since with the same line of 
> reasoning, I feel like one could decline any sort of Code of Conduct as 
> too radical and that it would split communities.

Let's not discuss code of conduct here, it's a separate and very
complex issue which doesn't belong to the subject of this thread.  A
distant analogy, maybe, but too distant.

> 1. The copyright questions seem to continue to be unresolved, even for 
> some small snippets: 
> https://fsfe.org/news/2026/news-20260825-01.en.html (I'm not a lawyer so 
> I can't judge this for myself, but I'd like to additionally express my 
> confusion why this article doesn't conclude "it seems best for projects 
> to not touch this tech for now"..)

As have been explained, we (and the entire GNU Project) are waiting
for lawyers to provide their recommendations, and for the GNU Project
leadership to translate them into practical guidance.  There's no
point in discussing this aspect until that happens, because none of us
here are lawyers.

> 2. It seems like AI can real harm on its users.

You mean, using Emacs whose code was generated in part by LLM or with
LLM assistance can harm Emacs users? how can that happen?

> Now you might argue you 
> can avoid it personally, but can everyone? You could say its the 
> responsibility of every contributor, but that may not always work out, 
> so I think a risk for the project itself is undeniable, even if low.

What is the risk for the project?   And how will rejecting
LLM-generated code mitigate that risk?

> 3. Higher risk for long term maintenance also seem pretty clear, since 
> human reviews apparently often can't keep up with the amount of code LLM 
> contributors produce.

I disagree that there's a significant risk of this, so "pretty clear"
is definitely not right.  There are no signs that we cannot keep up,
only fears that aren't based on any real evidence from the Emacs
development practice.

I explained elsewhere why examples from other projects are rarely
relevant to the unique situation in Emacs development.

> 4. I saw elsewhere the comparison you don't ask if contributors support 
> slave labor in other ventures. But surely that's a bit different from 
> allowing some form of slave labor product to directly knowingly 
> contribute to your project. (Not just people who have that view, but a 
> product, often proprietary, that has this known association, directly 
> altering the code base.) I feel like that's a more direct impact worth 
> considering on a local project level.

Not sure I understand you, but we never ask the contributors which
tools they used to work on the code they submit.  We don't require
them to edit the source with Emacs, for example.  They can edit with
Vim or Ex or VSCode or MS Visual Studio -- as long as the code is
correct and useful and clean, we are okay with accepting it.

> I think an additional thing to consider here is that any choice, 
> including no AI policy or a lenient policy, may also split the 
> community, maybe even worse so.

Any policy change should consider potential disagreements, and I'm
sure we will do that in this case as well, so no problem here.

[[[ To any NSA and FBI agents reading my email: please consider    ]]]
[[[ whether defending the US Constitution against all enemies,     ]]]
[[[ foreign or domestic, requires you to follow Snowden's example. ]]]

  > Research has repeatedly shown that using LLMs to generate the results 
  > that someone wants will undermine their ability to learn new things, 
  > depriving themselves and the larger community from this hard-won 
  > knowledge. This is even more problematic for novices, who may have never 
  > had an opportunity to learn things the "old-fashioned" way.

It is plausible that learning to develop software using an LLM will
impede learning of how to write (or understand) software without one.
But what is the factual basis for asserting that this is inevitable?
Are we racing ahead of actual knowledge?

  >  Worse still, 
  > the LLM providers advertise their models as equivalent to a junior 
  > engineer, encouraging maintainers to forego the work of mentoring novice 
  > contributors;

How much explicit mentorship have we done in this decade?

                ; even the Linux kernel [developers have] now decided to abandon 
  > mentorship,

What exactly have those developers abandoned?  If it is an
organizational practice, what does (or did) that practice consist of?
I have no idea -- I have never been involved in developing Linux.

  > I've seen these problems play out in projects I'm involved with, 
  > projects I rely on, and projects I only hear about when the problems 
  > boil over. I've thus concluded that LLMs corrode the community practices 
  > that free software relies on.

That might often happen, but the conclusion you've stated is a big
leap from what we actually know.  To be convinced that we must use
drastic measures to avoid "problems" would call for a much clearer
idea of what these problems consist of, than is stated in the words
quoted above.

[[[ To any NSA and FBI agents reading my email: please consider    ]]]
[[[ whether defending the US Constitution against all enemies,     ]]]
[[[ foreign or domestic, requires you to follow Snowden's example. ]]]

  > The current plan is to see if we can upstream the feature, in which case
  > the question of naming will be different anyway depending on where in
  > emacs.git the feature lands.

Ok.

                                  We therefore don't have to bikeshed this
  > point anymore.

Bikeshedding means fussing about minor details of a feature.  The
feature's name is not a minor detail, because a good name is
important: it can help the users who could use it to find it.

Choosing a name that will help users find it is a significant part of
making the feature useful.  If you don't want to participate in it,
stand aside and let those who care do the work.

  > > But allowing the use of LLM opens the door to getting much more of
  > > such contributions, and can quickly overwhelm a small team with
  > > amounts of code they now need to maintain without help.

  > As long as the code is well understood when it is accepted, and it's

  > problem any more than what we have now.

I agree: just because code was generated by an LLM does not imply it is
hard to understand.  Each such patch may be understandable, or not.

On that issue, we know how to deal with LLM-written code -- as if it
were written by someone we need to supervise.  We would have to be
disciplined and do it without fail, not get lulled into taking it for
granted.

>> After reading Bug#81908, I still don't quite understand what this patch
>> intends to avoid and how it works.  I understand that the `dash` package
>> might be a concrete case, tho maybe it needs its `dash-functional` "subpackage"
>> thrown into the mix, but it's still fairly fuzzy.  Could you describe
>> the shape of the problem in more detail?
>
> If packages foo and bar, where bar depends on foo are developed within
> the same repository, installing foo using package-vc would scan the
> repository for Package-Requires headers and find that bar depends on foo
> (the package being installed).

Hmm... why does it perform such a scan?

I'd have expected that it looks at the `Package-Requires:` header of the
main file only.

> The consequence therefore would be that we would install foo, the
> tarball, before installing foo, the VC package, and end up in
> a situation with both of these packages installed.

I see.

We could also keep `foo` in a list of "being installed" packages to
break the loop.  But circular dependencies should normally not happen,
so the loop shows up only because of the extra scan, IIUC.

>> Hmm... why does it perform such a scan?
>> I'd have expected that it looks at the `Package-Requires:` header of the
>> main file only.
>
> ./A
> =E2=94=9C=E2=94=80=E2=94=80 A-1.el      ;; Package-Requires: ((A "0"))
> =E2=94=9C=E2=94=80=E2=94=80 A-2.el      ;; Package-Requires: ((A-1 "0") (=
B "0"))
> =E2=94=94=E2=94=80=E2=94=80 A.el        ;; Package-Requires: ()
>
> If we only look at A.el only, A-2.el's dependency on B will be ignored.

I don't see why that's the problem: the users asked to install A only.
The fact that `A-2.el` happens to end up in the `load-path` is just an
"internal detail".

If they want to use A-2 as well, they should install it (which
presumably would add a symlink from directory `A-2` to directory `A`
and then look at the headers of `A-2.el`, ...).

Of course, we could be more proactive: *after* installing `A` (and hence
consulting the headers of `A.el`), we could scan the other files and ask
the users whether they also want to install those.

[ Note also that I've seen files `FOO.el` with headers like
  `Package-Requires:` even when there's no intention to make a package
  FOO out of it, so the scan risks finding packages that don't exist.  ]


=3D=3D=3D Stefan

Please take a look at the source code of vibe-spell.  I am half way
through it and it is certainly readable, certainly no worse than that of
the average ELPA submission.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/astoff/vibe-spell/refs/heads/main/vibe-spell.el

The "preferred form" question is a category error here, since the
translation is one between two forms of equal standing and not
comparable to machine-code output.  My guess is that the LLM would most
probably be able to recover a fully functional C++ version from the
Elisp code without much more difficulty in a way that a even a
decompiler wouldn't be able to do.

I would really appreciate it if we could give this whole business a rest
because at this point it is just noise.  I am sorry to tell you this,
but vibe-spell seems to be a good example of responsibly using LLMs that
doesn't result in so-called "slop" (which I understand to be some
horrible plague that nobody must ever come into contact with) and would
most probably never have been attempted without the availability of such
tools.

> Cheers

>>>> Hmm... why does it perform such a scan?
>>>> I'd have expected that it looks at the `Package-Requires:` header of t=
he
>>>> main file only.
>>>
>>> ./A
>>> =E2=94=9C=E2=94=80=E2=94=80 A-1.el      ;; Package-Requires: ((A "0"))
>>> =E2=94=9C=E2=94=80=E2=94=80 A-2.el      ;; Package-Requires: ((A-1 "0")=
 (B "0"))
>>> =E2=94=94=E2=94=80=E2=94=80 A.el        ;; Package-Requires: ()
>>>
>>> If we only look at A.el only, A-2.el's dependency on B will be ignored.
>>
>> I don't see why that's the problem: the users asked to install A only.
>> The fact that `A-2.el` happens to end up in the `load-path` is just an
>> "internal detail".
>>
>> If they want to use A-2 as well, they should install it (which
>> presumably would add a symlink from directory `A-2` to directory `A`
>> and then look at the headers of `A-2.el`, ...).
>>
>> Of course, we could be more proactive: *after* installing `A` (and hence
>> consulting the headers of `A.el`), we could scan the other files and ask
>> the users whether they also want to install those.
>>
>> [ Note also that I've seen files `FOO.el` with headers like
>>   `Package-Requires:` even when there's no intention to make a package
>>   FOO out of it, so the scan risks finding packages that don't exist.  ]
>
> That would certainly also be an option, but my design decision when
> implementing this was to be more careful and install all dependencies in
> case they are necessary.  The change we are discussing just tries to
> improve this overcorrection by a bit.  Another idea would be to prompt
> the user what dependencies they want to have installed.

An intermediate point would be to auto-install the dependencies listed
in the main file, and then prompt for the ones listed in the
other files (and, only after the installation of the package is done,
to avoid the circularity).

On Tue, Nov 10, 2026 at 12:24:23AM +0100, Dr. Arne Babenhauserheide wrote:
> Philip Kaludercic <philipk@posteo.net> writes:
>=20
> > The "preferred form" question is a category error here
>=20
> I=E2=80=99m not sure I understand correctly what you want to say with tha=
t.
>=20
> Do you mean it=E2=80=99s impossible to define a preferred form for modify=
ing?

I think this shows the weakness of the "GNU model" wrt the current
situation. For Philip it's perfectly OK for "an LLM" working along
a human. The human fixes and enhances directly the .el file, and
whenever a change worth backporting arrives in the C++, it tells the
LLM "please, LLM, backport this fix to me".

(Generative) LLMs and humans peacefully working together (please,
Philip, don't take this as sarcasm -- it just took me a while to wrap
my brain around that). Then, of course, there is no "preferred
source", that would be an anthropocentric view.

Me (and possibly Arne) stand squarely [1] in this anthropocentric place.
The GNU implicitly does, because it was conceived at a time nothing
else made sense. It'll have to change.

> Or that both versions form the preferred form together?
> To make it viable to transfer improvements from the one into the other.
> Can=E2=80=99t do that if you can=E2=80=99t diff to the shared state.

Not without LLM help. You do create a dependency.

Cheers

[1] I'll do for as long as this tech is dominated by Dark Lords.
--=20
t

"Dr. Arne Babenhauserheide" <arne_bab@web.de> writes:

> Philip Kaludercic <philipk@posteo.net> writes:
>
>> The "preferred form" question is a category error here
>
> I=E2=80=99m not sure I understand correctly what you want to say with tha=
t.
>
> Do you mean it=E2=80=99s impossible to define a preferred form for modify=
ing?

No, I am saying it doesn't make sense to talk about a "preferred form",
since we are not dealing with a compiler.

> Or that both versions form the preferred form together?

No, each version is independently sufficient to make changes.  This has
nothing to do with LLMs, just imagine any program that was translated
from language X to language Y.  There is no reason you can't just
continue developing the program in language Y after it has been
translated.

> To make it viable to transfer improvements from the one into the other.
> Can=E2=80=99t do that if you can=E2=80=99t diff to the shared state.

I cannot parse your claim here.  If there is a new feature in program X,
you take a look at the diff and re-implement the feature in program Y.
If the translation is faithful, as I understand to be the case with
vibe-spell, it is easier since you probably can match function names,
but otherwise you just re-implement the feature.  "OK, so language X now
also opens the file /etc/foo and check for a flag, sure can write that
too in language Y".  I really don't get the confusion here?

> Best wishes,
> Arne
