Philip Kaludercic <philipk@posteo.net> writes:

>> To make it viable to transfer improvements from the one into the other.
>> Can=E2=80=99t do that if you can=E2=80=99t diff to the shared state.
>
> I cannot parse your claim here.  If there is a new feature in program X,
> you take a look at the diff and re-implement the feature in program Y.
> If the translation is faithful, as I understand to be the case with
> vibe-spell, it is easier since you probably can match function names,
> but otherwise you just re-implement the feature.  "OK, so language X now
> also opens the file /etc/foo and check for a flag, sure can write that
> too in language Y".  I really don't get the confusion here?

The described process is: "point <tool> at <source diff>".

Not "tell <tool> to implement <described feature>".

That=E2=80=99s why whatever tool is used requires both sources: you need to=
 know
what C++ the elisp corresponds to to know what changed. At the very
least you need a reference to the exact commit that got processed.

Sure, you could try another way, but that=E2=80=99s not what Augusto plans =
to
do and not how he worked until now, so viability is speculation.

(not to forget in all the details: as long as there are no fully free
 tools that can do this (there are no fully free LLMs), this intended
 process adds a dependency on a proprietary tool as requirement to keep
 sources in sync, as well as deep copyright infringement risks if
 training data got reproduced with too little obfuscation)

Best wishes,
Arne

hei=C3=9Ft politisch sein,
ohne es zu merken.

submission rates growing up at the rates LLMs allow for, then this point=20

Hi!

On 31/10/2026 09:18, Eli Zaretskii wrote:
>> Date: Sat, 31 Oct 2026 07:02:25 +0200
>> Cc:monnier@iro.umontreal.ca,emacs-devel@gnu.org
>> From: Dmitry Gutov<dmitry@gutov.dev>
>>
>> On 30/10/2026 09:09, Eli Zaretskii wrote:
>>
>>> I was thinking about some kind of "memory", whereby if the last "M-g
>>> M-."  used some backend, the next one will use the same backend, with
>>> some command to reset the backend to the one that is the default for
>>> the current buffer's major mode.  The reason is that it happens a lot
>>> in my workflows that one tag search is followed by another, then
>>> another, etc., because I'm looking for something and didn't yet find
>>> it.  For example, I could be looking at a function which calls
>>> another, which in turns calls another, etc. etc., and I will be going
>>> down this rabbit hole because I need to understand something buried
>>> deep in a sequence of calls.  Or I could be looking for something,
>>> discover that it wasn't what I wanted, then change the symbol name
>>> slightly and search again, and so on and so forth, until I find what
>>> I'm looking for.  In these situations, having the backend change
>>> half-way is unexpected and annoying.
>> I see. Usually when doing something like that I would jump back each
>> time before next search, or use the Xref buffer to launch searches.
>>
>> But neither is very intuitive, I guess.
>>
>>> If you think that a minor mode which will allow this is reasonable,
>>> maybe that's good enough.  Another possibility would be to have a
>>> special value of prefix arg (e.g., "C-u C-u") to use the same backend
>>> as previous invocation, with a user option to reverse the meaning of
>>> "C-u C-u".
>> Would the use of 'C-u C-u' always make the commands prompt for
>> identifier to use.
> It would (and for the KIND as well), but that's usually what I need in
> these workflows, which chases some code until the answer is found.
> And the default for the symbol it offers is the symbol at point, so if
> that's what I want, it's only 2 keystrokes away.

Here is a draft with change that follows your description: 'C-u C-u M-.' 
uses the last "jump from" location as the origin for backend info.

There are a few rough edges:
- Unclear if this should work with every xref command. That would mean 
more potential clashes with others' prefix effects, and a need to 
document this somewhere in a common place. OT2H the benefits are there too.

- No support for defaulting to the symbol at point (it uses whatever 
symbol is in the previous buffer). If the command didn't interpret the 
given prefix convention to always mean "prompt for identifier", this 
would make a difference, . But I'm not sure how allow to pass both 
modifiers independently. 'M-- C-u'?

Or this could be a separate command or set of commands. Maybe a keymap. 
repeat-mode wouldn't help, though, if I understand your usage: any 
intervening commands would break out of it. So some prefix seems 
inevitable. Unless we add a command (e.g. a mode) that switches to this 
way of operation until the mode is disabled.

> Nov 9, 2026 17:08:22 Richard Stallman <rms@gnu.org>:
> 
> >   > As long as the code is well understood when it is accepted, and 
> > it's
> >   > clean and designed reasonably well, I don't see why this would be a
> >   > problem any more than what we have now.
> >
> > I agree: just because code was generated by an LLM does not imply it is
> > hard to understand.  Each such patch may be understandable, or not.
> >
> > On that issue, we know how to deal with LLM-written code -- as if it
> > were written by someone we need to supervise.  We would have to be
> > disciplined and do it without fail, not get lulled into taking it for
> > granted.
> 
> Cryptic code wasn't my main point of concern that I tried to 
> communicate.  It is the amounts of code team will have to process and 
> maintain - LLMs make it that the act of "writing the code" is the easy 
> part, which allows a lot more code to be submitted (see the recent 
> discussion on vibespell, for an example). Reviewing and maintaining such 
> amounts of code, submitted over the years may become problematic for a 
> small team. And because (as I pointed earlier) authors may not understand 
> the code they sent, expanding the team with new members to manage all 
> that code can become a problem too.

Please leave this problem to us, the Emacs maintainers.  It is our job
to make sure code doesn't get installed without proper review.  (An
exception is changes installed by people who have write access to the
Git repository and are trusted to install code without review.)  If
and when we see a problem with the amount of submitted changes, we
will do whatever is necessary to deal with that: limit submissions,
look for more reviewers, etc.

> I understand, that Emacs already has a lot of code, and it is already a 
> thing to deal with for the current team. Accepting LLM based 
> contributions just may make it much worse in the long run.

There's no reason to assume that we will be unable to cope with this,
if and when it happens.

> IMO, it's a point to be discussed, hence why I brought it up - if the 
> team is collectively OK with that they will have to deal with code 
> submission rates growing up at the rates LLMs allow for, then this point 
> can be dismissed.

We are okay, at least as long as this issue is just a theory for us.
Let's wait until something like that actually happens, and take it
from there.

[[[ To any NSA and FBI agents reading my email: please consider    ]]]
[[[ whether defending the US Constitution against all enemies,     ]]]
[[[ foreign or domestic, requires you to follow Snowden's example. ]]]

  > > as a hypothetical example: if i live in a territory that permits
  > > slavery, and by law i am granted sole ownership of the products of that
  > > forced labor, and then i use that to create contributions to gnu emacs,
  > > complete with copyright assignment, and it is technically correct, and,
  > > above all, you, the emacs maintainers are aware of how this was
  > > produced, would it be ethical to accept those contributions?

  > Our answer must be YES.

  > Any other answer is a first step towards splitting our community along
  > the many lines of political and ideological divides that have nothing
  > to do with software freedoms.  Right now we have contributors from all
  > over the world, despite the differences in their regimes and political
  > systems, differences in ideologies, and even in the very
  > interpretation of the notion of "freedom".  You are suggesting to
  > subject the contributors to some examination of the principles they
  > uphold, the ethics of their day-to-day activities, their views on
  > matters of policies and important international events, etc.  This
  > will immediately fracture our community into many different enclaves.

The right not to be a slave is a fundamental human right.  We should
refuse to participate in activities that involve owning slaves,
or treating anyone like a slave.

To refuse to use anything whose origin involved forced labor is much
harder.  If a road was built or is maintained with forced labor (such
chain gangs do exist in the US), do we have an obligation to refuse to
drive or ride on it?  I think that relationship is too indirect to
require rejection.  Also, I don't think that is an effective way to
campaign to put an end to forced prison labor.

The example that you're responding to is about where to draw the line
-- it was designed to be a borderline case.  In general, we wouldn't
know whether the developer of a contribution used slaves in its
development.  Is rejecting the contributions where we happen to know
about slaves a wise policy, if it surely goes with accepting a larger
number of contributions which were developed with slaves but we didn't
know?

We don't reject contributions from companies such as Google and Amazon
which are intentionally subjugating users.  These practices are not as
evil as outright enslavement, but they are plenty nasty nonetheless.
They don't literally force people to run their nonfree software, but
most people describe this as "impossible to resist".

Rejecting their useful contributions would not help us fight to stop
their unjust practices.  We may as well accept the former, as long as
we don't mute our condemnation of the latter.

-- 
Dr Richard Stallman (https://stallman.org)
Chief GNUisance of the GNU Project (https://gnu.org)
Founder, Free Software Foundation (https://fsf.org)
Internet Hall-of-Famer (https://internethalloffame.org)

[[[ foreign or domestic, requires you to follow Snowden's example. ]]]

  > > And yes, it is easy to write a script around Bison which will produce
  > > assembly or machine language directly.

I actually worked on Bison.  Generating assembly code or machine code
_for one target_ instead of C would be far more complex.
And we would need to port it to each machine architecture.
That would be enormous multiple duplication of effort.

  >   The fact that Bison produces C
  > > or C++ is just because of the Unix philosophy of each tool doing a
  > > single job, that's all.

We don't follow the "Unix philosophy".  In this particular
case, the modular design is better because it leads to
less code and requires less work to write, and less maintenance.

> From: Richard Stallman <rms@gnu.org>
> Cc: cwebber@dustycloud.org, phil@hagelb.org, arne_bab@web.de,
> 	jporterbugs@gmail.com, bugs@gnu.support, emacs-devel@gnu.org
> Date: Tue, 10 Nov 2026 09:31:38 -0500
> 
>   > Anyone who knows something about Emacs development and maintenance for
>   > the past decade or two can immediately see that the projects described
>   > in that blog are very different from what happens in Emacs nowadays.
>   > While the dangers described there are not unimaginable in Emacs, there
>   > are several factors that make them highly improbable.  One of them,
>   > perhaps the most important one, is that Emacs's codebase is very old
>   > and very stable, and that significantly affects the kinds of changes
>   > are being submitted most of the time, in ways that make those dangers
>   > much less likely to happen here.
> 
> I'm sure you have seen a real difference, but does that mean Emacs is
> inherently safe from this?  I could imagine a few people deciding to
> rewrite some part or aspect of Emacs in a radical way using nonfree
> tools.

As I said, it isn't unimaginable.  But it is quite rare in Emacs to
see such radical changes.  Moreover, if someone submits such a
changeset, we always have a lot of eyes will on it, because we want to
make sure such changes are in the right direction, well designed and
maintainable in the long run.  And because Emacs is a very complex
program with a lot of subtle aspects that no single person knows
enough about, we usually ask everyone who is an expert in some parts
of Emacs to review such patches.

You can take the recent example of adding an incremental GC to Emacs:
all the core developers and maintainers track that branch and
participate in the relevant discussions.  And because these cases are
rare in Emacs, it makes it possible for all those people to be part of
the discussions and provide valuable inputs and ides.

By contrast, the blog references in the message to which I responded
clearly talks about projects very early in their life cycle and with a
very different dynamics: they still frequently add major features,
they are under a constant pressure to put out significant features and
improvements in order not to "lose the race" to competing packages and
products, etc. etc. -- all of these things are very different from our
development dynamics.

I'm not saying the danger doesn't exist, I'm saying that our
development dynamics and practices make it significantly smaller
because many factors that urge people to use LLM-generated code more
and more don't exist here.

Historically, C-c was reserved for users' personal commands.
Emacs should have better default key bindings. This is not a feature;
it is a lack of respect for the keyboard.

For example, in python.el in Emacs 31.1. [[file:/usr/share/emacs/31.1/lisp=
/progmodes/python.el::(defvar-keymap python-base-mode-map]]

This begins with C-p and C-b, which cause the most confusion for
beginners and slow down not-very-smart long-time users.

More aggressive refactoring or death.

My suggestions:
 1) Don't use C-c in major modes.
 2) Research some soft recommendations that will arrange keybinds
 more standardly across built-in modes.
 3) (optional) Get rid of C-p and C-b by clearly suggesting to users
 from the first manual that they choose their own keys.
 Also, C-u and C-h should more conventionally follow *nix.

=2D-=20
Best regards,
.
Python+Java+Bash+Lisp Data Scientist, AI Engineer

> From: Anoncheg <vitalij@gmx.com>
> CC: 
> Date: Tue, 10 Nov 2026 15:19:04 -0000
> 
> 
> Historically, C-c was reserved for users' personal commands.

That's not accurate.  The ELisp manual says about this:

     • Don't define ‘C-c LETTER’ as a key in Lisp programs.  Sequences
       consisting of ‘C-c’ and a letter (either upper or lower case; ASCII
       or non-ASCII) are reserved for users; they are the *only* sequences
       reserved for users, so do not block them.

       Changing all the Emacs major modes to respect this convention was a
       lot of work; abandoning this convention would make that work go to
       waste, and inconvenience users.  Please comply with it.

     • Function keys <F5> through <F9> without modifier keys are also
       reserved for users to define.

     • Sequences consisting of ‘C-c’ followed by a control character or a
       digit are reserved for major modes.

     • Sequences consisting of ‘C-c’ followed by ‘{’, ‘}’, ‘<’, ‘>’, ‘:’
       or ‘;’ are also reserved for major modes.

     • Sequences consisting of ‘C-c’ followed by any other ASCII
       punctuation or symbol character are allocated for minor modes.
       Using them in a major mode is not absolutely prohibited, but if you
       do that, the major mode binding may be shadowed from time to time
       by minor modes.

So only "C-c <LETTER>" sequences are reserved for users.

> Emacs should have better default key bindings. This is not a feature;
> it is a lack of respect for the keyboard.
> 
> For example, in python.el in Emacs 31.1. [[file:/usr/share/emacs/31.1/lisp/progmodes/python.el::(defvar-keymap python-base-mode-map]]
> 
> This begins with C-p and C-b, which cause the most confusion for
> beginners and slow down not-very-smart long-time users.

This is in agreement with the above guidelines for major modes.

> My suggestions:
>  1) Don't use C-c in major modes.
>  2) Research some soft recommendations that will arrange keybinds
>  more standardly across built-in modes.
>  3) (optional) Get rid of C-p and C-b by clearly suggesting to users
>  from the first manual that they choose their own keys.
>  Also, C-u and C-h should more conventionally follow *nix.

I think it's too late to change these conventions that are in place
for several decades, and generations of Emacs users have them burned
into their muscle memories.  We'd be lynched if we change such basic
bindings.

Anoncheg <vitalij@gmx.com> writes:

> Historically, C-c was reserved for users' personal commands.
> Emacs should have better default key bindings. This is not a feature;
> it is a lack of respect for the keyboard.
>
> For example, in python.el in Emacs 31.1. [[file:/usr/share/emacs/31.1/lisp/progmodes/python.el::(defvar-keymap python-base-mode-map]]
>
> This begins with C-p and C-b, which cause the most confusion for
> beginners and slow down not-very-smart long-time users.
>
> More aggressive refactoring or death.
>
> My suggestions:
>  1) Don't use C-c in major modes.

Conventionally, C-c C-... prefix has been that of major modes, while C-x
... is that for global commands.  If you take a look at any larger major
mode (AucTeX, Proof General, SLIME, ...) they all use C-c
C-... extensively and it would be a massive undertaking and major
annoyance to change that.

>  2) Research some soft recommendations that will arrange keybinds
>  more standardly across built-in modes.
>  3) (optional) Get rid of C-p and C-b by clearly suggesting to users
>  from the first manual that they choose their own keys.
>  Also, C-u and C-h should more conventionally follow *nix.

Stefan Monnier <monnier@iro.umontreal.ca> writes:

>>>>> Hmm... why does it perform such a scan?
>>>>> I'd have expected that it looks at the `Package-Requires:` header of =
the
>>>>> main file only.
>>>>
>>>> ./A
>>>> =E2=94=9C=E2=94=80=E2=94=80 A-1.el      ;; Package-Requires: ((A "0"))
>>>> =E2=94=9C=E2=94=80=E2=94=80 A-2.el      ;; Package-Requires: ((A-1 "0"=
) (B "0"))
>>>> =E2=94=94=E2=94=80=E2=94=80 A.el        ;; Package-Requires: ()
>>>>
>>>> If we only look at A.el only, A-2.el's dependency on B will be ignored.
>>>
>>> I don't see why that's the problem: the users asked to install A only.
>>> The fact that `A-2.el` happens to end up in the `load-path` is just an
>>> "internal detail".
>>>
>>> If they want to use A-2 as well, they should install it (which
>>> presumably would add a symlink from directory `A-2` to directory `A`
>>> and then look at the headers of `A-2.el`, ...).
>>>
>>> Of course, we could be more proactive: *after* installing `A` (and hence
>>> consulting the headers of `A.el`), we could scan the other files and ask
>>> the users whether they also want to install those.
>>>
>>> [ Note also that I've seen files `FOO.el` with headers like
>>>   `Package-Requires:` even when there's no intention to make a package
>>>   FOO out of it, so the scan risks finding packages that don't exist.  ]
>>
>> That would certainly also be an option, but my design decision when
>> implementing this was to be more careful and install all dependencies in
>> case they are necessary.  The change we are discussing just tries to
>> improve this overcorrection by a bit.  Another idea would be to prompt
>> the user what dependencies they want to have installed.
>
> An intermediate point would be to auto-install the dependencies listed
> in the main file, and then prompt for the ones listed in the
> other files (and, only after the installation of the package is done,
> to avoid the circularity).

Sure, if there were a need for this, we can implement a user option to
that effect, but I suspect that it is not really needed.  I am guessing
it would have the following values:

- no-dependencies
- manual-selection
- main-automatic
- all-automatic

If any further bug reports follow up on this, it would make sense to
follow up on it, but until then _I_ am fine with the current
over-approximation that this change will have hopefully improved on.

One thing we also have to keep in mind is that any prompting will annoy
people who use the :vc keyword for use-package, since I understand
people want to use this to automatically bootstrap a configuration from
just an init.el.

On Tue, Nov 10, 2026 at 2:03=E2=80=AFPM Dr. Arne Babenhauserheide <arne_bab=
@web.de>
wrote:

>
> The process Augusto wants to use.
>

This is a misreading, or perhaps a mis-remembering.


> If the intention is to effectively cherry-pick changes from nuspell
> diffs through LLM,


That might be true, but it's not "the intention". What the OP actually said
was basically "IFF in the future there is some patch to the C version that
I want to include in the elisp version, I *could* do that by asking an agen=
t
to absorb both versions and generate an elisp patch, rather than by just
having the agent start over from scratch".

This is important in the context of agent-assisted coding, because, at
least in semi-recent practice, it is unfortunately common for coding
agents to "fix problems" by starting over, at least for large sections of
a codebase.

I saw no evidence of anyone claiming either an intention or a desire
to address all, most, or even necessarily any changes to the elisp
version by reverting partially or wholly to the C version; the poster
was instead saying that, in the case that there is a specific change
to the C code, the problem of "rewriting large chunks of the code"
(a current version of the CADT problem) can be avoided.

This distinction has given rise to different peoples having distinct
conversations "past" one another, an unfortunately common
occurrence, especially in on-line conversations. I hope that my
addition will help defray that; if I am unsuccessful, please
accept my apologies to all involved for adding to the volume.

I hope this helps,
~Chad

Top-posting to keep this thread from blowing up:

Abstractly speaking, there may be multiple methods to achieve a goal.
For software freedom we are concerned with the existence of plausible
method to achieve the goal which doesn't depend on non-free software.
If a maintainer decides to use another method, that is their choice, but
that doesn't matter.  Do we at least agree on that?

Concretely speaking, nothing about vibe-spell requires anyone to use
non-free software to change the software or even to backport changes.
It is NOT unreasonable to do so by hand, it will just take you
comparatively more time -- the decision of a maintainer to take this
path or another is entirely their own, and we cannot force a maintainer
to use free software as long as their choice doesn't require others to
not do so.  Are we on the same page on this point as well?

Philip Kaludercic <philipk@posteo.net> writes:

> Top-posting to keep this thread from blowing up:

No need to include the rest below for that. I can look back to previous
messages. That=E2=80=99s pretty nice with E-Mail.

> Abstractly speaking, there may be multiple methods to achieve a goal.
> For software freedom we are concerned with the existence of plausible
> method to achieve the goal which doesn't depend on non-free software.

There=E2=80=99s an important distinction: we don=E2=80=99t just need a plau=
sible, but a
practical way. A way that has not been shown repeatedly to fail.

> If a maintainer decides to use another method, that is their choice, but
> that doesn't matter.  Do we at least agree on that?

Only on the condition that that choice does not make it harder for
people to take over without unfree software.

> Concretely speaking, nothing about vibe-spell requires anyone to use
> non-free software to change the software or even to backport changes.
> It is NOT unreasonable to do so by hand, it will just take you
> comparatively more time -- the decision of a maintainer to take this
> path or another is entirely their own, and we cannot force a maintainer
> to use free software as long as their choice doesn't require others to
> not do so.  Are we on the same page on this point as well?

That depends on the definition of "require". People can mod proprietary
software, and are doing that every day with games. But we do not
consider doing only binary releases and locking away the source as
permissible for GNU maintainers.

Therefore "require" can=E2=80=99t mean "it is in theory possible to use Free
Software, but it won=E2=80=99t work well". The condition must be stronger. =
For
example: The tool the maintainer uses must not make it impractical for
other people to work on the package with purely Free Software.

Actually still stronger than that: a pure Free Software system should be
the best-supported one.

We=E2=80=99re talking about GNU packages after all, not just about adhering=
 to
the GPL=E2=80=99s legal terms.

And in the hermes discussion it was claified that a GNU package must not
encourage people to use proprietary software.

All LLM code I reviewed to date made usage with Free Software harder
than the equivalent handwritten code.

Best wishes,
Arne

hei=C3=9Ft politisch sein,
ohne es zu merken.

Content-Type: text/plain


I understand that some of these questions boil down to your agent
instructions.  I don't understand, for instance why you want to prefer
named-let over cl-doiter/cl-loop, since the former requires you to
iterate over the list and maintain the tail which I think that the
latter abstract over.

I haven't read the C++ code, but it doesn't seem like it is that C++-y.
Perhaps in some places it uses `if'-chains where `and' or a `cond' might
be more adequate, but that is not always the case and other functions
idiomatically use `or' instead of multiple `if' checks that each might
return nil.

It might be that you are re-implementing existing functionality, and
that might also be due to the translation that "proper" Elisp would use
a regular expression where you implement the logic in Lisp, but that is
a common mistake.

The flags abstraction wasn't clear to me, or if it even was an
abstraction but having a dictionary with some 50 fields feels like there
should be some room for improvement.  My guess is that this was a
bitfield in C++ that we can replace by a list encoding a set of symbols
or a bitvector with some nicer abstraction so that you don't have to
check for (/= ... 0) all the time.

But other than that, there was nothing fishy about the code and I think
it would be a nice addition.

To open a can of worms at the end, it might not be a bad idea to use a
different name for the package.  My hunch is that some of the attention
this thread has attracted is due to the name that has a negative
connotation.  The approach to spelling is sound after all, it is not
just a "vibe-check".  What do you think of "espell"?

--=-=-=--

terms of waiting for guidance it's to em actually enforcing being 
passive, since a lot of coders seem to be jumping the gun right now if 
not stopped.

In fact, the first LLM translation of C++ came full of catch/throw and
cl-block/cl-return (which uses the same internally).  It turns out that
catch/throw is substantially slower -- but only when native compiled.

So I picked a non-catchy looping construct.

--8<---------------cut here---------------start------------->8---
(defmacro dolist-until (spec &rest body)
  "Like `dolist', but stop when BODY first evaluates to a non-nil value.
When that happens, evaluate RESULT and return it.  If RESULT is omitted,
return the last body value.

\(fn (VAR LIST [RESULT]) BODY...)"
  (declare (indent 1) (debug ((symbolp form &optional form) body)))
  (unless (consp spec)
    (signal 'wrong-type-argument (list 'consp spec)))
  (unless (<=3D 2 (length spec) 3)
    (signal 'wrong-number-of-arguments (list '(2 . 3) (length spec))))
  (let ((var (car spec))
        (tail (make-symbol "tail"))
        (result (make-symbol "result")))
    `(let ((,tail ,(nth 1 spec)) ,var ,result)
       (while ,tail
         (setq ,var (car ,tail))
         (setq ,result ,(macroexp-progn body))
         (setq ,tail (if ,result
                         ,(when (length=3D spec 3)
                            `(prog1 nil
                               (setq ,result ,(macroexp-progn (cddr spec)))=
))
                         (cdr ,tail))))
       ,result)))
--8<---------------cut here---------------end--------------->8---

With no RESULT argument it replaces seq-some, and with RESULT =3D VAR it
replaces seq-find.

I've used this macro for a while, then decided to just go with a
standard ELisp construction instead (and chose named-let due to cl-loop
allergy).

I'm not entirely convinced, but maybe that macro might be generally
useful?

> abstraction but having a dictionary with some 50 fields feels like there
> should be some room for improvement.  My guess is that this was a
> bitfield in C++ that we can replace by a list encoding a set of symbols
> or a bitvector with some nicer abstraction so that you don't have to
> check for (/=3D ... 0) all the time.

To make sure we're on the same page, flags are e.g. the PY in this .dic
entry:

  amorphous/PY

the meaning of the flags is defined in the .aff file.  I don't know what
P is, but Y means "out can append ly" to get amorphously.

So yes, this flag handling looks un-idiomatic to me but maybe it's close
to optimal.  I haven't fully understood it.

> But other than that, there was nothing fishy about the code and I think
> it would be a nice addition.

Nice!

> To open a can of worms at the end, it might not be a bad idea to use a
> different name for the package.  My hunch is that some of the attention
> this thread has attracted is due to the name that has a negative
> connotation.  The approach to spelling is sound after all, it is not
> just a "vibe-check".  What do you think of "espell"?

Will reply separately.

Here I would appreciate the opinion from Arne and the others with
concerns about LLM-generated code.  Do you think I should rename the
package?

I named it that way 1. as an attempt to be a bit funny, in a
self-deprecating way, and 2. to not let anybody have the wrong idea
about the method used to write that large (but not unreasonable large)
amount of code.  I certainly didn't mean to be provocative.

(I don't want to expound on my opinion about LLMs here, but I have fun
in actually writing ELisp and I'm not on the Emacs payroll or following
deadlines, so this package to me is a rather special experiment.  All my
other packages are and will remain handcrafted.)

Hi again.

Sorry if I'm insisting on this...

I had ten minutes today and wrote a **TOY** (attached) just to learn to 
do RPC in Python. I took a couple of functions from the API I saw in 
jinx-mod.c and tried to implement something that would communicate 
through RPC in a similar way as jinx interacts with the enchant library.

Now the next step would be to write the Emacs part. I think it shouldn't 
be too difficult, since eglot already has a lot of jsonrpc that could be 
used to inspire the glue needed. No agent, no nothing.

In this case, we have the additional goodie of offloading the burden of 
keeping up with the enchant/aspell/hunspell evolution on the libraries 
used by the toy, not on the toy itself.

This is only a toy and I was using Python because I'm lazy. Now select a 
set of libraries, languages, etc. with a good old compliant license that 
cover the major OSes and there you are.

No need for fierce discussions ;-)

using `catch'.  I would argue that at least for you use-case, it would
be nice to have this macro so that you can abstract over the list
management logic.

that I would imagine you'd have people requesting dolist-when,
dotimes-when, etc.  If you abstract over all of these special case
macros you end up with cl-loop :)

>
> Here I would appreciate the opinion from Arne and the others with
> concerns about LLM-generated code.  Do you think I should rename the
> package?
>
> I named it that way 1. as an attempt to be a bit funny, in a
> self-deprecating way, and 2. to not let anybody have the wrong idea
> about the method used to write that large (but not unreasonable large)
> amount of code.  I certainly didn't mean to be provocative.

If it is intentional, then I guess it should be fine.  My concern was
mostly that "vibe" is nowadays commonly used as a put-down phrase, so
it sounded to me like calling the package "bad-spell".  But then
again, packages by the names of "dumb-jump" and "evil" exist :)

I think that if the concern is to indicate that a package is LLM
generated, we can add metadata to the package itself and have package.el
respect+indicate it, it doesn't necessarily have to be communicated
using the name.

> (I don't want to expound on my opinion about LLMs here, but I have fun
> in actually writing ELisp and I'm not on the Emacs payroll or following
> deadlines, so this package to me is a rather special experiment.  All my
> other packages are and will remain handcrafted.)

On 11/9/2026 6:04 AM, Richard Stallman wrote:
> It is plausible that learning to develop software using an LLM will
> impede learning of how to write (or understand) software without one.
> But what is the factual basis for asserting that this is inevitable?
> Are we racing ahead of actual knowledge?

﻿I've followed at a distance some of the research on this over the last 
few years. From what I've seen, the research consistently concludes that 
LLMs hurt learning and overall cognition. Here's a selection of papers 
on the topic.

First is "How AI Impacts Skill Formation" 
<https://arxiv.org/pdf/2601.20245>. This was published by Anthropic 
researchers in Feb 2026 and compares users learning a new Python library 
by themselves or with a chatbot they can query, so it's closely relevant 
to our situation. (Since it's Anthropic, if there's any bias, it's 
likely in favor of LLMs as a useful assistant for programming.)

Their top-line results show a statistically-insignificant reduction in 
task completion time (23min with AI, 25 without, p=0.391), but the 
reduction in test score *is* statistically-significant (50% with AI, 66% 
without, p=0.010).

Before I go any farther, I should note that this is a fairly small 
study, at n=52 (26 each in the AI and no-AI groups). However, there are 
a few interesting details beyond the top-line results. First, there's 
almost no difference in task completion time, except for novices (1-3 
years experience). See Figure 7. Broken down by age, the average test 
score is the reverse: very close for 1-3 years experience, but wider for 
other levels (again though, this is statistically weak due to the small 
population size).

The study also suggests there are a few interaction patterns that can 
produce better results: "Generation-Then-Comprehension", "Hybrid 
Code-Explanation", and "Conceptual Inquiry" (see Figure 11 and the 
nearby text). Compared to the lower-scoring patterns, these ones had 
greater emphasis on asking questions than having the chatbot do the 
work. *However*, these groups are n=2, n=3, and n=7 respectively, and 
I'll additionally note that Fig 11 has no error bars. Statistically 
speaking, I don't think you can put much weight on this; again, even the 
full population is quite small at n=52.

Finally, the authors also note in Section 7.1 that, "This should be a 
lower bound for cognitive offloading since agentic AI coding tools would 
require even less human participation." A common objection with research 
like this is that the tools are so much more advanced now, but the 
authors hypothesize here that these advancements would make it even 
harder to learn. (And in any case, marketing doesn't override science 
just because it has a more recent publication date.)

Here are some additional papers with similar results. I haven't looked 
at these in as much detail, so I'm only providing a quick blurb about each:

----------------------------------------

Endoscopist deskilling risk after exposure to artificial intelligence in 
colonoscopy: a multicentre, observational study (Oct 2025)
<https://doi.org/10.1016/S2468-1253(25)00133-5>

This paper observed the endoscopists had worse performance doing 
non-AI-assisted colonoscopies after having spent 3 months using AI 
assistance.

----------------------------------------

Thinking—Fast, Slow, and Artificial: How AI is Reshaping Human Reasoning 
and the Rise of Cognitive Surrender (Feb 2026)
<https://doi.org/10.31234/osf.io/yk25n_v1>

This paper introduces the idea of "cognitive surrender": when using AI, 
users "often surrender to its outputs—whether correct or flawed."

----------------------------------------

Sycophantic AI decreases prosocial intentions and promotes dependence 
(Mar 2026)
<https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aec8352>

This one is about interpersonal interactions, but the results are quite 
disturbing: "In our human experiments, even a single interaction with 
sycophantic AI reduced participants’ willingness to take responsibility 
and repair interpersonal conflicts, while increasing their own 
conviction that they were right. Yet despite distorting judgment, 
sycophantic models were trusted and preferred."

----------------------------------------

AI Tools in Society: Impacts on Cognitive Offloading and the Future of 
Critical Thinking (Jan 2025)
<https://doi.org/10.3390/soc15010006>

I believe this paper is mostly based on self-reports from the study 
participants, so you may want to take it with a grain of salt. Still, 
the authors conclude: "The findings revealed a significant negative 
correlation between frequent AI tool usage and critical thinking 
abilities, mediated by increased cognitive offloading."

----------------------------------------

AI-overdependence and human cognitive decline: Hazards, evidence, and 
mitigation strategies (May 2026)
<https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chbr.2026.101102>

This paper reviews the literature on AI's cognitive effects over the 
last few years, and according to the authors, "reveals that 
AI-overdependence poses a significant threat to higher-order cognitive 
skills, especially critical thinking, complex decision-making, and 
analytical reasoning, while also undermining creativity, memory, and 
executive functions. These effects stem from well-documented mechanisms 
such as cognitive offloading, metacognitive laziness, and automation 
bias, compounded by the perceived authority and convenience of AI systems."

----------------------------------------

 From Offloading to Engagement: An Experimental Study on Structured 
Prompting and Critical Reasoning with Generative AI (Oct 2025)
<https://doi.org/10.3390/data10110172>

This is the most-positive paper I could find after a brief search, and 
suggests that "structured prompting" avoids some of the problems with 
cognitive offloading. This structured prompting consists of restricting 
LLM use to looking up contextual or factual information, and then later 
prompting the LLM to generate counterarguments for their essay. However, 
the study only uses self-reporting to measure the level of cognitive 
offloading, so I'd again take this with a grain of salt. Even with the 
comparatively optimistic views of the author, they note, "The study 
highlights this risk of an illusion of non-offloading: even individuals 
with strong critical dispositions may fail to recognise their reliance 
on AI, accepting outputs as anchors while believing they have remained 
independent."

----------------------------------------

While it takes a long time to come to true scientific consensus, 
especially with a technology like LLMs that are seeing such frequent 
changes, current research is pointing towards LLM use having significant 
cognitive and learning harms. Given all of that, I prefer to apply the 
precautionary principle. Maybe in the future, the situation will change, 
but I'd rather wait until there's a reasonable amount of research that 
has happier results than the above papers.

[[[ To any NSA and FBI agents reading my email: please consider    ]]]
[[[ whether defending the US Constitution against all enemies,     ]]]
[[[ foreign or domestic, requires you to follow Snowden's example. ]]]

  > I don't see how this is different from reviewing any other
  > contribution.  When I review a patch, the amount of effort invested by
  > the contributor has no effect on my efforts.  And I always need to
  > invest some effort to understand the changes.

The reviewer has no obligation to continue studying the proposed patch
for however much time it takes to understand it.  If it is hard to
understand, you can reject it for that reason, or say "It is not clear
how this code works, so I can't accept it.  Please explain the code
with clear comments."

If the contributor is unable to write a clear explanation, you don't
have much more work to do on that patch.

If the only way to understand some a patch is to use an LLM that is
nonfree or SaaSS, then since morally we reject using that, it follows
that understanding that patch is impossible for us, so we must reject
it.

  > > When we get a submission of code, we almost always ask questions and
  > > request some changes.  What do you think will happen if in response we
  > > get "blank stares"?

  > Very likely the maintainers will find themselves indirectly talking to
  > an LLM. This is just my naive opinion, but to me this doesn't sound
  > like it would allow for a very healthy community.

  also

  > It's quite difficult to explain if you haven't experienced it firsthand,
  > but LLM-generated code and explanations are astonishingly good at
  > *looking* correct and being extremely convincing at first glance in a
  > way that is completely disconnected to whether it is correct or not.

I suggest that, instead of discussing whether the patch is correct, we
say that the code lacks explanation to make its meaning clear clear,
and ask the contributor to add clear explanation.  "Tell us what X
means here", for instance.

That way we won't get into the kind of argument that LLMs could fool
people at.

  > > 3. Higher risk for long term maintenance also seem pretty clear, since 
  > > human reviews apparently often can't keep up with the amount of code LLM 
  > > contributors produce.

In order to maintain human control over the Emacs code base, we must
refuse to be hurried in dealing with proposed changes.  That means we
must refuse to feel hurried by whatever would-be contributors say or
do.  We must set the pace so that we can do the job properly.

Emacs.  Not only for moral reasons, but also because code we don't
understand cannot be in Emacs since it could then do stuff we don't
want Emacs to do.

> 
> I can't make any sense of that.  It looks like Eli rejected the
> offered code because it was not clear.  Eli, can you tell us any more
> of what you were thinking when you read that message?

I rejected the explanations of the root cause(s) of the problem
because they made no sense to me, given my familiarity with how the
display engine works.  I also pointed out why the explanations made no
sense.  Since they made no sense, whether to accept patches was never
on the table, because the patches were based on assumptions and
conclusions which couldn't be correct, as they disregarded basic
principles of how the display engine works.

> If we will reject such unclear patches and unclear explanations as Eli
> did this time, does that constitute an adequate way way of handling
> them?

I don't see why it won't.

In general, both in my work on Emacs and elsewhere in my life, I never
completely reject any idea or utterance, because almost always there's
something useful in there.  Even if the idea is completely false, it
can frequently give me correct ideas as I think about why and how it
is false.  The source of the ideas is never too important (except that
if I know from experience that a particular source has high
probability of generating false ideas, I will scrutinize ideas from
such a source with some prejudice).  Therefore, I cannot agree with
people who say that LLM-generated text should be ignored as garbage,
because it could include useful parts or lead me to useful ideas as I
consider what it tells.

That's what I did in this case: rejected the wrong ideas and the
patches offered based on those wrong ideas after showing with code
fragments why they cannot be true.  Thus, "talking to LLM" allowed me
to examine the code in Emacs and attempt to find problems there which
could explain the issues discussed in that bug report.

Note that, among a lot of incorrect hypotheses and suggestions which
were posted "from LLM's mouth" in that discussion, one was close to
the real cause of the problem, but failed to identify the place where
the code should be corrected.  That place was later identified by
Sameer Singh and the problem was fixed where it happens.  My
conclusion from this was that thinking about what LLM tells is useful,
because some, even if small, part of what it says could give useful
ideas.  When dealing with code in Emacs we are less familiar with,
that could help identify and solve problems which otherwise might
remain unsolved.

Which is what happens already in Emacs, and was always so.

Accepting changes without proper review, just because the author
hurries us, would be doing a bad job.  When the contributor pings us,
we try to make more time for reviewing the contribution, but we don't
do it less thoroughly.

Richard Stallman <rms@gnu.org> writes:

> [[[ To any NSA and FBI agents reading my email: please consider    ]]]
> [[[ whether defending the US Constitution against all enemies,     ]]]
> [[[ foreign or domestic, requires you to follow Snowden's example. ]]]
>
>   > Like with many SaaS products, LLM vendors have been caught admitting
>   > that they deliberately design the flow of these systems with the goal=
 of
>   > being addictive, so it's not particularly surprising that this happen=
s.
>   > The only surprise is that people who should know better continue to f=
all
>   > for it.
>
> Can you send us links to pages about these admissions?
> This is the sort of thing that could be a rumor; before citing it
> as the basis for a conclusion, I'd like to verify it.

The primary source is a document that was leaked to 404 media:

https://www.404media.co/microsoft-wants-to-make-people-addicted-to-scout-it=
s-new-ai-assistant-internal-documents-reveal/

This article requires a login to read, but it doesn't require payment. I
can quote the relevant part:

> The internal Microsoft document, called =E2=80=9CClawPilot: Overview and =
Plan
> with Project Lobster,=E2=80=9D seen by 404 Media has a subheading called
> =E2=80=9CClawPilot Overall Plan,=E2=80=9D which notes =E2=80=9Cthree phas=
es=E2=80=9D to its launch
> plan. The first phase is =E2=80=9CMake people addicted.=E2=80=9D
>
> =E2=80=9CContinue shipping the standalone ClawPilot experience. Pilot the=
 UX,
> grow the user base, and build the skill and tool ecosystem that makes
> people depend on it daily. This is already happening organically,=E2=80=
=9D the
> document says. Omar Shahine, the Microsoft executive leading the
> project, adds that in its pilot with Microsoft employees, they have
> seen =E2=80=9CDaily Usage with High Retention and intensity of usage (cha=
ts,
> queries, workflows, skills).=E2=80=9D

Not particularly surprising behavior coming from Microsoft.

Here's another article on the topic that doesn't require a login:

https://futurism.com/artificial-intelligence/microsoft-plots-addicted-to-it=
s-ai

>   > I know this looks at first glance like a slippery slope fallacy, but =
I'm
>   > just describing what happened from painful firsthand personal experie=
nce.
>   > I have read about the same thing happening in multiple free software
>   > projects as well,
>
> Do you know of any free software project that has faced this problem
> and prevented it?

The only prevention I know to be effective is a clear and unambiguous
ban on LLM contributions, which I've applied to all the projects I
run. I don't know of a project which has avoided these problems without
a ban. I have read about projects like the game engine Bevy where they
had a ban but then lifted it, and it went very badly:

https://blog.fallible.net/it-breaks-a-village/

Projects like this where they try to find a middle ground and require
that LLM usage must be "responsible" or "human guided only" don't
usually end up successful in those criteria over time due to the "vibe
bobsled" problem I mentioned earlier.

=2DPhil

> From: Phil Hagelberg <phil@hagelb.org>
> Cc: arne_bab@web.de,  eliz@gnu.org,  jporterbugs@gmail.com,
>   bugs@gnu.support,  emacs-devel@gnu.org
> Date: Wed, 11 Nov 2026 22:33:15 -0800
> 
> > Do you know of any free software project that has faced this problem
> > and prevented it?
> 
> The only prevention I know to be effective is a clear and unambiguous
> ban on LLM contributions, which I've applied to all the projects I
> run. I don't know of a project which has avoided these problems without
> a ban. I have read about projects like the game engine Bevy where they
> had a ban but then lifted it, and it went very badly:
> 
> https://blog.fallible.net/it-breaks-a-village/

AFAICT, there are no technical issues described in that blog, only
social ones.  They are described very vaguely (probably because the
audience is supposed to be familiar with the details), but from what I
could understand, the policy change to allow LLM-generated code was
done without sufficient discussions and consent, and that and the
following social dynamics caused severe problems like distrust and
break of communications between members of the community.

Whether this could happen to us if LLM-generated code is allowed
depends on us, not on LLMs or the code they generate.  I want to hope
that we will be wise enough to keep communications channels open,
good-faith and trustworthy, and to avoid alienating one another
because of our differing opinions.  I don't see why someone who is
okay with using LLMs should distrust or despise someone who dislikes
them, or vice versa.  I also don't see why the differences in opinions
on these matters could justify a fork, which is an extreme expression
of breakage in social relationships which hold communities together.
I've seen this when XEmacs forked, and my conclusions back then was
that, although the reasons were presented as technical ones, they were
not.

> Projects like this where they try to find a middle ground and require
> that LLM usage must be "responsible" or "human guided only" don't
> usually end up successful in those criteria over time due to the "vibe
> bobsled" problem I mentioned earlier.

That this is likely to happen, let alone inevitable, has never been
sufficiently demonstrated in the context of Emacs development or
anything similar.  So I still don't see why it should be regarded as
being anywhere near certainty.

> >   > It's quite difficult to explain if you haven't experienced it firsthand,
> >   > but LLM-generated code and explanations are astonishingly good at
> >   > *looking* correct and being extremely convincing at first glance in a
> >   > way that is completely disconnected to whether it is correct or not.
> > 
> > I suggest that, instead of discussing whether the patch is correct, we
> > say that the code lacks explanation to make its meaning clear clear,
> > and ask the contributor to add clear explanation.  "Tell us what X
> > means here", for instance.
> > 
> > That way we won't get into the kind of argument that LLMs could fool
> > people at.
> 
> This is *precisely* what generative LLMs are getting pretty good at.
> 
> The contributor passes the maintainer's questions to the LLM and sends
> back its answers.

Please read the discussion in bug#82057.  That's what happened there,
but based on that I cannot say that the particular LLM used is "pretty
good at" explaining itself.  It didn't take me long to find and expose
the fallacies in those explanations.  After the 3rd iteration of that,
I pointed out to the contributor that I'm not willing to continue that
way anymore, with the result that the next response was much shorter
and to the point, because it provided an easily followed recipe and
almost completely dropped the bogus explanations of why the problem
happens.

> The maintainer is faced to do a constant Turing test which is becoming
> harder and harder.

I didn't find that to be "harder and harder".  I found it to be very
similar to talking to some humans around here (which will remain
unnamed).  So when I faced that bug's discussion, I could draw on
real-life experience.  When you read some description of what some
code does, and you are familiar enough with that code, it doesn't take
long for you to spot fallacies, and then disregard everything based on
the fallacies.  At least IME, this usually allows to analyze a message
of several hundred lines very quickly.

And please don't go the way of saying I have some exceptional
experience or abilities, because I don't.  I've seen Sean and others
deal with similar situations no less efficiently.

Once again, I think you and others who post similar messages
underestimate the Emacs maintainers and their abilities.  The need to
deal with a crowd such as this one, day in and day out, teaches us
something that can be efficiently applied to the envisioned situations
with LLM-generated stuff (again, provided that GNU allows that at some
point).  And neither are we ignorant of what LLMs can and cannot do.

Now, I don't know why the developers of those projects described in
those blogs were different and let these bad things happen, but I do
now us, and I'm not afraid.

>
> Now the next step would be to write the Emacs part. I think it

(I just released jit-spell with support for different backends (at the
moment vibe-spell and "ispell -a") so you can plug and play your toy if
you want).

> In this case, we have the additional goodie of offloading the burden
> of keeping up with the enchant/aspell/hunspell evolution on the
> libraries used by the toy, not on the toy itself.
>
> This is only a toy and I was using Python because I'm lazy. Now select

Sure this can be done, and if you provided prebuilt binaries for every

than a pure-ELisp implementation?

mentioned somewhere upthread, I think an FFI for Emacs would probably be
the best approach, better than jinx, vibe-spell or your approach.)

Indeed.

with LLM-generated stuff (again, provided that GNU allows that at some<br>
point).=C2=A0 And neither are we ignorant of what LLMs can and cannot do.<b=
r>
<br>
Now, I don&#39;t know why the developers of those projects described in<br>
those blogs were different and let these bad things happen, but I do<br>
now us, and I&#39;m not afraid.<br>

[[[ To any NSA and FBI agents reading my email: please consider    ]]]
[[[ whether defending the US Constitution against all enemies,     ]]]
[[[ foreign or domestic, requires you to follow Snowden's example. ]]]

  >  It is the amounts of code team will have to process and 
  > maintain - LLMs make it that the act of "writing the code" is the easy 
  > part, which allows a lot more code to be submitted

We do the best we can feasibly do, with the pile of bug reports and
patches we receive.

Just because a person sends us a proposed change, it does not follow
that we _have to_ look at it.  When we do look at a change, it does
not follow that we _have to_ study it until we understand it.  We
could instead let it drop.

If a message shows us there is a bug, and presents a proposed fix, we
can use that fix if we can understand it and be sure it is correct.
We also have the possibility of fixing that bug another way, if that
is easier.  If we can't understand it, we may have to let it drop.

  > IMO, it's a point to be discussed, hence why I brought it up - if the 
  > team is collectively OK with that they will have to deal with code 
  > submission rates growing up at the rates LLMs allow for, then this point 
  > can be dismissed.

I think these are independent issues:

1. Will people send us more proposed patches because THEY use LLMs?

2. Will Emacs get a lot bigger because of OUR installing patches
made by LLMs?

> This is okay, but we should also suppress the warning in the code
> which loads these files, because people might have such old files
> lying around.  Can you add that?

I considered that, but didn't add it (yet) because I think the remedy to
this warning is easy: Just let RefTeX reparse the file with

  M-x reftex-parse-all RET

and RefTeX will update it .rel file when .tex file is killed; no editing
of the .tex file is needed.

Does this make sense?

Richard Stallman <rms@gnu.org> writes:

>   > IMO, it's a point to be discussed, hence why I brought it up - if the 
>   > team is collectively OK with that they will have to deal with code 
>   > submission rates growing up at the rates LLMs allow for, then this point 
>   > can be dismissed.
>
> I think these are independent issues:
>
> 1. Will people send us more proposed patches because THEY use LLMs?

This is bound to happen because generating patches with a coding agent
is basically one prompt, if Emacs allows LLM-generated contributions.
For example, to fix a bug, you describe the problem to it and ask for a
patch.  The coding agent will autonomously study the code, change the
code, and validate that the symptom is fixed (not necessarily the root
cause).

I co-maintain an open-source project which does not ban LLM-generated
contributions (only requiring "responsible use"), and I see much more
pull requests nowadays.  I have very mixed feelings because, while some
PRs make perfect sense, many don't.

> 2. Will Emacs get a lot bigger because of OUR installing patches
> made by LLMs?

IME, most LLM-generated patches will be about fixing bugs and improving
performance.  Patches that add features are rare, and they are most
likely rejected anyway because they are usually designed badly and don't
fit into the bigger picture.

FYI, in Org mode mailing list, we did not say anything about LLMs for a
long time, yet receiving just a handful of LLM-generated patches.

patches. Just because the number of LLM-generated submissions was too
small to even bother.

barrier to filter out people who do not want to bother figuring out how
to send a patch to mailing list. But my evidence is anecdotal (single
project). We are yet to see what happens with Emacs, where the number of
contributions is much higher.

Eli Zaretskii <eliz@gnu.org> writes:

>> Richard Stallman <rms@gnu.org> writes:
>> 
>> >   > IMO, it's a point to be discussed, hence why I brought it up - if the 
>> >   > team is collectively OK with that they will have to deal with code 
>> >   > submission rates growing up at the rates LLMs allow for, then this point 
>> >   > can be dismissed.
>> >
>> > I think these are independent issues:
>> >
>> > 1. Will people send us more proposed patches because THEY use LLMs?
>> 
>> This is bound to happen because generating patches with a coding agent
>> is basically one prompt, if Emacs allows LLM-generated contributions.
>> For example, to fix a bug, you describe the problem to it and ask for a
>> patch.  The coding agent will autonomously study the code, change the
>> code, and validate that the symptom is fixed (not necessarily the root
>> cause).
>
> You assume that someone will set up an LLM to automatically respond to
> all the Emacs bug reports with patches?

Not at all.  I'm simply predicting that there will be more patches,
(because they become very cheap).

> If not, then the usual problem with bugs is not to produce a fix, it's
> to take notice of it.  The bug list is routinely read only by the
> Emacs maintainers and not many other people.

I agree.  On the other hand, my understanding is that many people here
are worried that the maintainers would have to spend more time dealing
with LLM-generated prose and code, and risk burnout.  But of course this
is up to the maintainers to decide for themselves.

>> I co-maintain an open-source project which does not ban LLM-generated
>> contributions (only requiring "responsible use"), and I see much more
>> pull requests nowadays.  I have very mixed feelings because, while some
>> PRs make perfect sense, many don't.
>
> What prevents you from rejecting those which don't make sense?

Nothing.  They are rejected as they should be.  :-)

(Perhaps off-topic) For our project, personally I do not want a ban on
LLMs because some external contributions are wondrous.  Heck, some
performance optimization opportunities could easily take a human months
to find and implement, or maybe never, because no living creature can
know C++ inside out.  And who doesn't like faster software?

I guess dealing with more nonsense is a price we have to pay?  Or maybe
something like the vouch system [1] can let us have a sustainable
community while not turning down every LLM-generated contribution?  I
really cannot tell.

[1] https://github.com/mitchellh/vouch

> Not at all.  I'm simply predicting that there will be more patches,
> (because they become very cheap).
> 
> > If not, then the usual problem with bugs is not to produce a fix, it's
> > to take notice of it.  The bug list is routinely read only by the
> > Emacs maintainers and not many other people.
> 
> I agree.  On the other hand, my understanding is that many people here
> are worried that the maintainers would have to spend more time dealing
> with LLM-generated prose and code, and risk burnout.  But of course this
> is up to the maintainers to decide for themselves.

People who worry that our workload will increase should consider
coming aboard to help with that.  This will be greatly appreciated
even today, before all of the above might happen.

In any case, rejecting a certain class of change proposals without
reviewing them, just because it helps with the workload, doesn't sound
like a good strategy to me.

> I guess dealing with more nonsense is a price we have to pay?

Yes.  And that is no different from making contributions easier to
submit, something that happened when Emacs switched from CVS to Bazaar
and later to Git.  We should welcome more contributions, and we should
be (and AFAICT already are) able to quickly recognize nonsense and
discard it.

> Or maybe something like the vouch system [1] can let us have a
> sustainable community while not turning down every LLM-generated
> contribution?  I really cannot tell.
> 
> [1] https://github.com/mitchellh/vouch

Personally, I would be against such a system.  It is basically a kind
of public shaming, and IME shaming based on these criteria is bad for
the community, as it begets unhealthy social dynamics, with all that
comes with it.  It is not a coincidence that when we decide to reject
a contribution, we use very soft language where we try very hard to be
positive so as not to lose the contributor, and sometimes do that
off-list.

[[[ To any NSA and FBI agents reading my email: please consider    ]]]
[[[ whether defending the US Constitution against all enemies,     ]]]
[[[ foreign or domestic, requires you to follow Snowden's example. ]]]

More important than the name of the package is what it contains and what
that implies about its further development.

Please correct me if I'm mistaken, but it seems that further
maintenance of vibe-spell will require running the same LLM on future
versions of hunspell, to generate new versions of the code in
vibe-spell.  Not just once, not just five times, but over and over.

That LLM is a SaaSS dis-service, right?

It might turn out ok to use source code that was (past tense)
generated by an LLM.  (Our interim policy is to refuse.)  But we
certainly can't have Emacs virtually include, or suggest using, a
program whose maintenance depends on repeatedly updating its source
code by running a nonfree or SaaSS LLM again and again.  Emacs
development would be lastingly dependent on that LLM.

In that scenario, we can't rationally assert that the use of that tool
was done by someone else in the past and we are not morally
responsible for it.  We must reject that kind of dependence by
rejecting vibe-spell.

[[[ To any NSA and FBI agents reading my email: please consider    ]]]
[[[ whether defending the US Constitution against all enemies,     ]]]
[[[ foreign or domestic, requires you to follow Snowden's example. ]]]

More important than the name of the package is what it contains and what
that implies about its further development.

Please correct me if I'm mistaken, but it seems that further
maintenance of vibe-spell will require running the same LLM on future
versions of hunspell, to generate new versions of the code in
vibe-spell.  Not just once, not just five times, but over and over.

That LLM is a SaaSS dis-service, right?

It might turn out ok to use source code that was (past tense)
generated by an LLM.  (Our interim policy is to refuse.)  But we
certainly can't have Emacs virtually include, or suggest using, a
program whose maintenance depends on repeatedly updating its source
code by running a nonfree or SaaSS LLM again and again.  Emacs
development would be lastingly dependent on that LLM.

In that scenario, we can't rationally assert that the use of that tool
was done by someone else in the past and we are not morally
responsible for it.  We must reject that kind of dependence by
rejecting vibe-spell.

[[[ To any NSA and FBI agents reading my email: please consider    ]]]
[[[ whether defending the US Constitution against all enemies,     ]]]
[[[ foreign or domestic, requires you to follow Snowden's example. ]]]

  > Returning back to the actual package, I read the entire source and
  > collected a few comments and suggestions here:


  > [2:text/x-patch Hide]

  > diff --git a/vibe-spell.el b/vibe-spell.el
  > index e28eb68..aac30da 100644
  > --- a/vibe-spell.el
  > +++ b/vibe-spell.el
  > @@ -97,11 +97,13 @@ Donaudampfschiffahrtselektrizitätenhauptbetriebswerkbauunterbeamtengesellschaft
  >    "Maximum word length to be processed by the spell checker.
  >  Longer words are always reported as correct.")
 
  > +;; Shouldn't this be a user option?
  >  (defvar vibe-spell-check-time-limit 5
  ...

Some of the changes you suggest are more substantial than mere comments.
That shows we need to resolve the question of how vibe-spell relates
to hunspell.  We've considered two paths:

1. vibe-spell is treated as a form of hunspell, and we intend
to transpose (all, or many) future hunspell changes into vibe-spell.

  a. That will sometimes be done using an LLM.

  b. That will always be done by a human.

2. vibe-spell is an independent program now, and its future development
will not be tied to that of hunspell, though one might get inspiration
from new hunspell features.

There could also be a path 1.5 which is a "sometimes 1 and sometimes
2", but it would raise the same issues as path 1, so we don't need to
treat it separately.

This is the fundamental moral decision we know of regarding vibe-spell.
Path 1a (or 1.5a) is unacceptable since it would tie future development
to a tool it is against our principles to use or recommend.

We could choose path 1b, or path 2, but will people actually follow
that decision, or would we be fooling ourselves?  I think that only
with some time can we tell the answer.  We need enough time for their
to be substantial changes in hunspell that people want to transpose
into vibe-spell.

Aside from this moral issue, there is also the legal issue of whether
this code can be copyrighted (and, therefore, copylefted).  We are
trying to find out, but having an answer may take time.

We must take the time needed for a good final decision.
We must wait and see.

Therefore, don't install vibe-spell now into NonGNU ELPA (or into GNU
ELPA).

When enough months have gone by to give us a basis for a thoughtful
decision, we should consider this question based on what we have seen.

[[[ To any NSA and FBI agents reading my email: please consider    ]]]
[[[ whether defending the US Constitution against all enemies,     ]]]
[[[ foreign or domestic, requires you to follow Snowden's example. ]]]

  > For software freedom we are concerned with the existence of plausible
  > method to achieve the goal which doesn't depend on non-free software.

That comes fairly close to part of our concerns, but it is not
complete and not properly formulated.  Don't use that statement's
wording as a basis for argument.

  > If a maintainer decides to use another method, that is their choice, but
  > that doesn't matter.  Do we at least agree on that?

In general, no.  That statement is sweepingly broad.  It is valid for
some issues, but there are others for which it is not valid.

It is valid for personal choices which have no effect on anyone else.
For instance, if you edit a file with a proprietary text editor, that
normally has no effect on anyone else, so we don't need to ask what
you did.

But there are various private actions whose consequences can affect
the program's other developers, its users, or the project overall.
--

[[[ To any NSA and FBI agents reading my email: please consider    ]]]
[[[ whether defending the US Constitution against all enemies,     ]]]
[[[ foreign or domestic, requires you to follow Snowden's example. ]]]

  > But the question wasn't about the ethical views of the contributor. It 
  > was about whether the contribution was produced by slave labour, not 
  > whether the contributor was in favour of slave labour.

People who force others to work as slaves deserve punishment.  In most
real countries, that is a crime and they can be punished by law.

If they used forced labor in a business, for profit, we can punish
them in a practical way by boycotting the business, and thus denying
them the profit they sought.  We should do that.

If they used forced labor to make something generally beneficial, and
the public did nothing to encourage or reward that use of forced
labor, they still deserve to be punished, for forcing slaves to work.

But the public does not deserve to be punished on their account.  A
campaign to reject that beneficial thing would hurt only the innocent
public.  There is no sense in that.  We should rather campaign to
properly punish the guilty ones.

-- 
Dr Richard Stallman (https://stallman.org)
Chief GNUisance of the GNU Project (https://gnu.org)
Founder, Free Software Foundation (https://fsf.org)

On 11/14/2026 2:13 PM, Richard Stallman wrote:
> [[[ To any NSA and FBI agents reading my email: please consider    ]]]
> [[[ whether defending the US Constitution against all enemies,     ]]]
> [[[ foreign or domestic, requires you to follow Snowden's example. ]]]
> 
>    > IMO, it shouldn't be a problem, provided that "the information it
>    > provides" doesn't include code that you then submit as the fix, with
>    > or without modifications.  IOW, "the information it provides" should
>    > be analysis of the bug and its reasons, and suggestions for fixes that
>    > don't include code.  At least that is my understanding.
> 
> I agree, but to make it clearer, I'd change "suggestions for fixes that
> don't include code" to "suggestions for approaches to use for fixes, not including code."

I have been experimenting with this. I suggest putting into AGENTS.md 
something like this:

"When the user describes a bug to fix or an improvement to implement:

- First, explain why the bug happens, including context about the 
internals, which the user may not know about.
- Only then, on the user's request, suggest strategies (approaches) to 
fix the bug. Don't choose one for the user.
- Never generate code."

The LMs I've used have a tendency to go all the way on the first call, 
and talk to me like I am an expert, for my ego I guess. This tames them 
somehow.

This is not a textual suggestion, I don't have the english.

> > [[[ foreign or domestic, requires you to follow Snowden's example. ]]]
> >
> >    > IMO, it shouldn't be a problem, provided that "the information it
> >    > provides" doesn't include code that you then submit as the fix, wi=
th
> >    > or without modifications.  IOW, "the information it provides" shou=
ld
> >    > be analysis of the bug and its reasons, and suggestions for fixes
> that
> >    > don't include code.  At least that is my understanding.
> >
> > I agree, but to make it clearer, I'd change "suggestions for fixes that
> > don't include code" to "suggestions for approaches to use for fixes, no=
t
> including code."
>
> I have been experimenting with this. I suggest putting into AGENTS.md
> something like this:
>
> "When the user describes a bug to fix or an improvement to implement:
>
> - First, explain why the bug happens, including context about the
> internals, which the user may not know about.
> - Only then, on the user's request, suggest strategies (approaches) to
> fix the bug. Don't choose one for the user.
> - Never generate code."
>
> The LMs I've used have a tendency to go all the way on the first call,
> and talk to me like I am an expert, for my ego I guess. This tames them
> somehow.
>
> This is not a textual suggestion, I don't have the english.
>

It could be acceptable for a user to ask an LLM to generate a *concise* and
*correct* report with a standalone *reproducer*, if the bug reporter can't
(or won't) do that on their own (laziness can be tantamount to
disrespect).  Many of the LLM submissions I've had to deal with on other
projects are verbose "brain dumps" and cost a lot of time to read through
and mine potential gems from the roughs.

On Sat, Nov 14, 2026 at 8:13=E2=80=AFAM Richard Stallman <rms@gnu.org> wrot=
e:

>
> Some of the changes you suggest are more substantial than mere comments.
> That shows we need to resolve the question of how vibe-spell relates
> to hunspell.  We've considered two paths:
>
> 1. vibe-spell is treated as a form of hunspell, and we intend
> to transpose (all, or many) future hunspell changes into vibe-spell.
>
>   a. That will sometimes be done using an LLM.
>
>   b. That will always be done by a human.
>
> 2. vibe-spell is an independent program now, and its future development
> will not be tied to that of hunspell, though one might get inspiration
> from new hunspell features.
>
> There could also be a path 1.5 which is a "sometimes 1 and sometimes
> 2", but it would raise the same issues as path 1, so we don't need to
> treat it separately.
>
> This is the fundamental moral decision we know of regarding vibe-spell.
> Path 1a (or 1.5a) is unacceptable since it would tie future development
> to a tool it is against our principles to use or recommend.
>
> We could choose path 1b, or path 2, but will people actually follow
> that decision, or would we be fooling ourselves?  I think that only
> with some time can we tell the answer.  We need enough time for their
> to be substantial changes in hunspell that people want to transpose
> into vibe-spell.
>

I thought Augusto put this to bed already opting for the ELisp source code
presiding.  See
https://lists.gnu.org/archive/html/emacs-devel/2026-11/msg00228.html

Aside from this moral issue, there is also the legal issue of whether
> this code can be copyrighted (and, therefore, copylefted).  We are
> trying to find out, but having an answer may take time.
>
> We must take the time needed for a good final decision.
> We must wait and see.
>
> Therefore, don't install vibe-spell now into NonGNU ELPA (or into GNU
> ELPA).
>

I thought one purpose of NonGNU ELPA was specifically to avoid copyright
assignment considerations as the code could be public domain (as all LLM
output might be considered) or otherwise freely licensed by authors without
assignment.  It says close to that here https://elpa.nongnu.org/about.html =
(and
is silent on other copyright considerations).

> > I thought Augusto put this to bed already opting for the ELisp source

> > https://lists.gnu.org/archive/html/emacs-devel/2026-11/msg00228.html

>

Either way, it's his choice, it's his package, and his contributions to
Emacs and community engagement have been welcome.

> I thought one purpose of NonGNU ELPA was specifically to avoid copyright
> assignment considerations as the
> > code could be public domain (as all LLM output might be considered) or
> otherwise freely licensed by authors
> > without assignment.
>
> The code could also be a copyright violation and everyone propagating it
> could be infringing on the copyright of authors of parts of the training
> data (because it would not have been legal that they got it).
>

It could be but that's irrelevant as the policy is to extend trust to
authors.  Even if LLM output is not copyrightable, it still can be valuable
work when shepherded by someone trustworthy with good taste.  Being a
copyright violation is a separate matter and proving such would require an
exhaustive search of all code publicly in the wild as published lyrics tend
to be (private code can never be infringed having never been used for
training).  Such author trust matters.  I'd rather not be here among this
crowd if there is distrust among our good contributors.  And let's give
Augusto some credit for being transparent and willing to subject himself to
this discussion.

See
>
> https://www.twobirds.com/en/insights/2025/landmark-ruling-of-the-munich-r=
egional-court-%28gema-v-openai%29-on-copyright-and-ai-training
> and
>
> https://www.gesetze-bayern.de/Content/Document/Y-300-Z-GRURRS-B-2025-N-30=
204
>
> The legal situation is currently in flux and we don=E2=80=99t know how it=
 will
> play out.
>

It's murkier than that, even.  In Singapore, materials used for model
training are not considered violations and to the degree Augusto chose a
model that was trained there and perhaps run there (at Megaspeed, for
example), he could be in the clear.  This is for the FSF lawyers to deal
with, not us, right?  And as Eli has said many times, let's set these aside
for now and focus on vibe-spell (or espell whatever it is now called) and
on Augusto's valuable contribution.

Eli Zaretskii <eliz@gnu.org> wrote:

>   Ping!  How can we make further progress in thismatter?

I think we have agreement on what the default should be for system
types other than MS Windows.  So let's look at Windows.

It appears that on Windows, system accounts are in the range
500 to 999, and user accounts start at 1000.

However, the groups situation appears to be more complicated.
All accounts, both Administrators and ordinary users, could
have groups in the 513+ range.  Probably on Windows we need to
ignore (or have a separate limit for) group ids.  A patch to
ignore gid on Windows is appended below.

As the simplest way forward now, I think if we changed the
"privileged" limit on Windows to 500 that it would be no worse
than the current limit.  Thus

  (if (memq system-type '(darwin cygwin windows-nt)) 500 999)


 < Stephen
